All of this generalizes our discussion around Definition 2.14, for which $R=\mathbb{S}$ .

#### Example 6.5 (Vector bundle twists).

We have been using (rank-zero virtual) vector bundles to define twists of bordism theories, and these two notions of twist are compatible: rank-zero virtual vector bundles $V\to X$ are classified by maps $f_{V}\colon X\to B\mathrm{O}$ , and the $J$ -homomorphism is a map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ ; then, if $\xi$ is a tangential structure with two-out-of-three data, the unit map $e\colon\mathbb{S}\to\mathit{MT\xi}$ induces a map $e\colon B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathit{MT\xi})$ . The Thom spectrum for $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -bordism, as we characterized it in Corollary 3.4, is naturally equivalent to the Thom spectrum $M(e\circ J\circ f_{V})$ of the map

$$ X\overset{f_{V}}{\longrightarrow}B\mathrm{O}\overset{J}{\longrightarrow}B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})\overset{e}{\longrightarrow}B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathit{MT\xi}). $$

This is a combination of theorems of Lewis [LMSM86, Chapter IX] and Ando-Blumberg-Gepner-Hopkins-Rezk (see [ABG+14a, Corollary 3.24] and [ABG+14b, §1.2]).

#### Theorem 6.7 (May-Quinn-Ray [May77, Lemma IV.2.6]).

There is a canonical null-homotopy of the map

$$ e\circ J\circ\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathit{MT\xi}), $$

and therefore $e\circ J$ factors through the cofiber $B\mathrm{O}/B$ , and in fact through $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B$ .

In other words, the homotopy type of the Thom spectrum for $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -bordism depends only on the image of $V$ in $B\mathrm{O}/B$ . And the key slogan is that the orders of elements in $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B]$ control the periodicity of families of Smith homomorphisms for twisted $\xi$ -bordism; the group structure on $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B]$ uses the fact that $B\mathrm{O}/B$ is the cofiber of a map of grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces, and $B\mathrm{O}$ is connected, so $B\mathrm{O}/B$ is also a grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -space (see [DY23a, §1.2.2]). Thus homotopy classes of maps into $B\mathrm{O}/B$ naturally form abelian groups.

#### Definition 6.9 (Bhattacharya-Chatham [BC22, Definition 2.9]).

The $\mathit{MT\xi}$ -orientation order of a virtual vector bundle $V\to X$ , written $\Theta(V,\mathit{MT\xi})$ , is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $V^{\oplus k}$ is $\mathit{MT\xi}$ -oriented, or infinity if no such $k$ exists.

Equivalently, $\Theta(V,\mathit{MT\xi})$ is the order of the classifying map of $e\circ J\circ f_{V}\colon X\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathit{MT\xi})$ , where $f_{V}\colon X\to B\mathrm{O}$ is the classifying map of $V$ . By Theorem 6.7, $e\circ J\circ f_{V}$ factors through $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B]$ , so $\Theta(V,\mathit{MT\xi})$ divides the exponent of $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B]$ . We will use this fact below to make quick estimates of orientation orders.

#### Proposition 6.10.

Let $V\to X$ be a vector bundle. If $\epsilon\coloneqq\Theta(V,\mathit{MT\xi})$ is finite, the Smith homomorphism family of $(X,kV)$ -twisted $\xi$ -bordism is $\epsilon$ -periodic.

This bound is not sharp, as we discuss in §6.4.

#### Proof.

The image $\overline{f_{V}}$ of the classifying map $f_{V}\colon X\to B\mathrm{O}$ in $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B]$ satisfies $(k+\epsilon)\overline{f_{V}}=k\overline{f_{V}}$ . Since the homotopy type of the Thom spectrum for $(X,W)$ -twisted $\xi$ -bordism only depends on $\overline{f_{W}}\in[X,B\mathrm{O}/B]$ , this implies that the notions of $(X,kV)$ -twisted $\xi$ -bordism and $(X,(k+\epsilon)V)$ -twisted spin bordism coincide, so the Smith family $\{(X,kV):k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is $\epsilon$ -periodic. ∎

### 6.2. Examples of periodic Smith families

Though Proposition 6.10 seems abstract, it lends itself readily to examples.

#### Example 6.11 (Unoriented bordism families are $1$ -periodic).

Proposition 6.10 implies that when $\xi=\mathrm{id}\colon B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}$ , the periodicity of a Smith family of $(X,kV)$ -twisted unoriented bordism divides the exponent of $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}]=0$ . In other words, all Smith families of twisted unoriented bordism are $1$ -periodic.

We will see some examples of Smith families for unoriented bordism in Examples 7.4, 7.24, and 7.41.

#### Example 6.12 (Oriented bordism families are $2$ -periodic).

Because $B\mathrm{SO}$ is the fiber of $w_{1}\colon B\mathrm{O}\to K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ , and the Whitney sum formula implies $w_{1}$ is a map of $E_{\infty}$ -spaces, the cofiber $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}$ is equivalent to $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ as grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces. Thus for all spaces $X$ , $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}]$ is annihilated by $2$ , so all Smith families for twisted oriented bordism are $2$ -periodic (or $1$ -periodic).

We will see some examples of Smith families for oriented bordism in Examples 7.6, 7.15, 7.24, 7.37, and 7.41.

#### Example 6.13 (Complex and spin $c$ bordism families are $2$ -periodic).

If $V$ is a real vector bundle, then $V\oplus V$ has a canonical complex structure (think of this bundle as $V\oplus iV$ ), and therefore also a canonical spin $c$ structure. Therefore for any map $f\colon X\to B\mathrm{O}$ , $2f$ lifts to $B\mathrm{U}$ and to $B\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ . Therefore the image of the map $[X,B\mathrm{O}]\to[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{U}]$ has exponent $2$ (and likewise for $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ ), so by Proposition 6.10 all Smith families of complex and spin $c$ bordism are at most $2$ -periodic.

For examples of Smith families for spin $c$ bordism, see Examples 7.13, 7.24, and 7.41 and Footnote 22.

#### Example 6.14 (Spin bordism families are $4$ -periodic).

$B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}$ is not equivalent to a product of Eilenberg-Mac Lane spaces even as an $E_{1}$ -space [DY23a, Lemma 1.37], so we cannot reuse the strategy of (6.12). However, there is a cofiber sequence of grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces (heuristically, an extension of abelian $\infty$ -groups) [DY23a, §1.2.3]

$$ K(\mathbb{Z}/2,2)\longrightarrow B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1), $$

inducing a long exact sequence on $[X,\text{--}]$ . Since $[X,K(\mathbb{Z}/2,2)]$ and $[X,K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)]$ both have exponent at most $2$ for any $X$ , exactness implies $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}]$ has exponent at most $4$ . Thus using Proposition 6.10 we conclude that all twisted spin bordism Smith families are at most $4$ -periodic; in fact, Example 7.8 has period exactly $4$ , which implies (6.15) does not split. One could also argue $4$ -periodicity similarly to Example 6.13.

If we restrict to oriented vector bundles, we can do better, as periodicity is controlled by maps into $B\mathrm{SO}/B\mathrm{Spin}\simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/2,2)$ (the argument is similar to $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}\simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ from Example 6.12). Therefore we conclude that twisted spin Smith families using an oriented vector bundle are $2$ -periodic.

We will discuss several examples of $1$ -, $2$ -, and $4$ -periodic Smith families for spin bordism in Examples 7.8, 7.28, 7.35, 7.37, 7.41, and 7.47.

#### Remark 6.16.

Periodicity for spin bordism also implies periodicity for $\mathit{ko}$ and $\mathit{KO}$ . Bhattacharya-Chatham [BC22, Main Theorem 1.5] generalize this periodicity of $\mathit{KO}$ -orientability to higher real $K$ -theories $\mathit{EO}_{\Gamma}$ .

#### Example 6.17 (Families of twisted string structures).

The space $B\mathrm{Spin}$ is $3$ -connected, with $\pi_{4}(B\mathrm{Spin})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ ; if one kills this homotopy group by taking the $4$ -connected cover, one gets a space $B\mathrm{String}$ , and the corresponding tangential structure is called a string structure [ST04, Definition 5.0.3] (see also [Gia71, §1]). The generator of $H^{4}(B\mathrm{Spin};\mathbb{Z})$ is not the first Pontrjagin class $p_{1}$ , but rather is a class $\lambda$ with $2\lambda=p_{1}$ [Tho62, Theorem 1.2]. Thus a string structure on a spin vector bundle is equivalent data to a trivialization of $\lambda$ .

As grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces, $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}$ is an extension of $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}$ by $B\mathrm{Spin}/B\mathrm{String}\simeq K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ (see [DY23a, §1.2.4]); since $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}$ is itself an extension of $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ by $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,2)$ , if $X$ is a $3$ -connected space, $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}]\cong H^{4}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ . Thus for a general space $X$ , Proposition 6.10 provides no information on Smith families for twisted string bordism: it reports that the period is at most infinity. We will nevertheless prove in Corollary 6.33 that all twisted string Smith families have finite period, though our proof does not provide an effective computation of the period.

In special cases, though, Proposition 6.10 allows us to provide sharper bounds: for example, because $H^{*}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z})$ is $2$ -torsion in positive degrees and $[B\mathbb{Z}/2,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}]$ has exponent $4$ , the long exact sequence associated to the cofiber sequence $K(\mathbb{Z},4)\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}$ implies $[B\mathbb{Z}/2,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}]$ has exponent at most $8$ , implying that all Smith families of $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,V)$ -twisted string bordism are at most $8$ -periodic; an $8$ -periodic example appears in Example 7.10.

### 6.3. Examples of twisted bordism

In this subsection, we discuss how to use the perspective we have been developing to concretely identify examples of twists of $\xi$ -bordism for the tangential structures $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , and $\mathrm{Spin}$ .

#### Lemma 6.18 (Shearing [ABG+14b, §1.2]).

If a twist $f\colon X\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(M\xi)$ factors through a map $g_{V}\colon X\to B\mathrm{O}$ classifying a rank-zero virtual vector bundle $V\to X$ as in (6.6), then $Mf\simeq\mathit{MT\xi}\wedge X^{V}$ .

We will use this lemma as follows: first, for the four tangential structures $\xi\colon BG\to B\mathrm{O}$ mentioned above, we compute the homotopy type of $B\mathrm{O}/BG$ and understand the map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}/BG$ , to recognize when a map $X\to B\mathrm{O}/BG$ comes from a (virtual rank-zero) vector bundle $V\to X$ . In that situation, Lemma 6.18 describes the corresponding twisted $\xi$ -bordism groups as $\Omega_{*}^{\xi}(X^{V})$ , so we can use the Smith homomorphism tools we developed in this paper.

#### Example 6.19 (Twists of oriented bordism).

Recall from Example 6.12 that $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}\simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ ; the argument there implies the map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}\xrightarrow{\simeq}K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ is the first Stiefel-Whitney class. Given a map $a\colon X\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}$ , the Thom spectrum of the corresponding twist $f_{a}\colon X\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{SO})$ of $MT\mathrm{SO}$ is the bordism spectrum whose homotopy groups are the bordism groups of manifolds $M$ with a map $\phi\colon M\to X$ and a trivialization of $w_{1}(M)-\phi^{*}(a)$ .1111 11 Strictly speaking, what one trivializes is $w_{1}(\nu)-\phi^{*}(a)$ , where $\nu\to M$ is the stable normal bundle, but there is a canonical identification of $w_{1}(M)$ and $w_{1}(\nu)$ . This nuance will matter for spin structures.

Every class $a\in H^{1}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is the first Stiefel-Whitney class of some line bundle $L_{a}\to X$ , so for any twist $f\colon X\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{SO})$ described by a map $f_{a}\colon X\xrightarrow{a}K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)\simeq B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{SO})$ , there is a homotopy equivalence

$$ Mf\xrightarrow{\simeq}MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge X^{L_{a}-1}. $$

For example, unoriented bordism is an example of such a twist: every manifold $M$ has a canonical map to $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ , given by $w_{1}(M)$ , and $w_{1}(M)-w_{1}(M)$ has a canonical trivialization. Therefore unoriented bordism is twisted oriented bordism for the twist $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)\xrightarrow{\simeq}B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{SO}$ , and Lemma 6.18 implies $MT\mathrm{O}\simeq MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge(K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1))^{\sigma-1}$ , where $\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2\simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)$ is the tautological line bundle; this is a theorem of Atiyah [Ati61a, Proposition 4.1].

For another example of how to use Lemma 6.18, let $\mathcal{W}$ denote the Thom spectrum for the notion of bordism of manifolds $M$ equipped with a lift of $w_{1}(M)$ to a class $\alpha\in H^{1}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ . The class $\alpha$ is equivalent to a map $\phi\colon M\to B\mathbb{Z}=S^{1}$ , and $\alpha=\phi^{*}x$ , where $x\in H^{1}(S^{1};\mathbb{Z})$ is the generator; rephrased in this way, the condition that $\alpha\bmod 2=w_{1}(M)$ is equivalent to a trivialization of $w_{1}(M)-\phi^{*}(x\bmod 2)$ . Therefore $\mathcal{W}$ -bordism is twisted oriented bordism for $(S^{1},x\bmod 2)$ , and as $x\bmod 2$ is $w_{1}$ of the Möbius bundle $\sigma\to S^{1}$ , we learn from Lemma 6.18 that $\mathcal{W}\simeq MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge(S^{1})^{\sigma-1}$ . This is also due to Atiyah [Ati61a, §4].

#### Example 6.21 (Twists of spin $c$ bordism).

There is an equivalence of spaces, but not $E_{1}$ -spaces, $B\mathrm{O}/B{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)\times K(\mathbb{Z},3)$ [DY23a, Proposition 1.20, Lemma 1.30], and the map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ is picked out by $(w_{1},\beta(w_{2}))$ , where $\beta$ is the integral Bockstein. The fact that $\beta(w_{2})$ is not linear in the direct sum of vector bundles is why this decomposition of $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ does not respect the $E_{1}$ -structure.

Given data $a\in H^{1}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and $c\in H^{3}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ , if $Mf_{a,c}$ is the Thom spectrum for the corresponding twist

$$ f_{a,c}\colon X\overset{(a,c)}{\longrightarrow}K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)\times K(\mathbb{Z},3)\simeq B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}), $$

then the homotopy groups of $Mf_{a,c}$ are the bordism groups of manifolds $M$ with maps $\phi\colon M\to X$ and trivializations of $w_{1}(M)-\phi^{*}(a)$ and $\beta(w_{2}(M))-\phi^{*}(c)$ ; the proof is essentially the same as Hebestreit-Joachim’s [HJ20, Corollary 3.3.8] (Footnote 11 still applies: what appears is the stable normal bundle, but the characteristic classes are the same). If there is a (rank-zero, virtual) vector bundle $V\to X$ with $w_{1}(V)=a$ and $\beta(w_{2}(V))=c$ , then Lemma 6.18 implies $Mf_{a,c}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge X^{V}$ and we can invoke the Smith homomorphism on $V$ .

For example, a pin $c$ structure on a manifold $M$ is a trivialization of $\beta(w_{2}(M))$ (i.e. the spin $c$ condition without the trivialization of $w_{1}$ ). Thus a pin $c$ structure is equivalent to a twisted spin $c$ structure where $X=B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , $a$ is the generator of $H^{1}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ , and $c=0$ : as in Example 6.19, $w_{1}(M)$ gives us a canonical map to $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , there is a canonical trivialization of $w_{1}(M)-w_{1}(M)$ , and $c=0$ means this twisted spin $c$ condition does not modify $\beta(w_{2})$ . So this twisted spin $c$ condition is that $\beta(w_{2})=0$ and $w_{1}$ is arbitrary, i.e. a pin $c$ structure. And if $\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the tautological line bundle, $w_{1}(\sigma)=a$ and $\beta(w_{2}(\sigma))=0=c$ , so Lemma 6.18 implies $MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\sigma-1}$ , reproving a theorem of Bahri-Gilkey [BG87a, BG87b].

Other examples of twists of spin $c$ bordism which can be realized by vector bundles include the spin- $\mathrm{U}(2)$ bordism of Davighi-Lohitsiri [DL20, DL21] and the tangential structure corresponding to Stehouwer’s alternate class AI fermionic groups [Ste22, §2.2].

Not every choice of $(a,c)$ can be realized by a vector bundle; for example, $\beta(w_{2})$ is always $2$ -torsion, but $c$ need not be. There are also examples with $2$ -torsion $c$ , as a consequence of work of Gunawardena-Kahn-Thomas [GKT89, §2].

#### Example 6.23 (Twists of spin bordism).

The most commonly studied examples of twisted $\xi$ -bordism in mathematical physics are twists of spin bordism. The story is closely analogous to Example 6.21, with $K(\mathbb{Z},3)$ replaced with $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,2)$ , and the map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}\simeq K(\mathbb{Z}/2,1)\times K(\mathbb{Z}/2,2)$ is $(w_{1},w_{2})$ . Given classes $a\in H^{1}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ and $b\in H^{2}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ , the homotopy groups of the Thom spectrum of the corresponding twist $f_{a,b}\colon X\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{Spin})$ are the bordism groups of manifolds $M$ with maps $\phi\colon M\to X$ and trivializations of $w_{1}(\nu)-\phi^{*}(a)$ and $w_{2}(\nu)-\phi^{*}(b)$ [HJ20, Corollary 3.3.8], where $\nu\to M$ is the stable normal bundle. Now, unlike in Footnote 11, the distinction between $TM$ and $\nu$ matters: $w_{1}(TM)=w_{1}(\nu)$ , but $w_{2}(TM)+w_{1}(TM)^{2}=w_{2}(\nu)$ , providing a formula for the nontrivial transition from tangential to normal data. If $a=w_{1}(V)$ and $b=w_{2}(V)$ for a rank-zero virtual vector bundle $V\to X$ , Lemma 6.18 implies $Mf_{a,b}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge X^{V}$ . See [DY23a, §1.2.3] for more information.

Many commonly studied tangential structures arise as vector bundle twists of spin structures.

- (1) A pin $-$ structure is a trivialization of $w_{2}(M)+w_{1}(M)^{2}$ , with no condition on $w_{1}$ . Thus this is equivalent to a trivialization of $w_{2}(\nu)$ . Like in Examples 6.19 and 6.21, we can ask for a map $\phi\colon M\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and a trivialization of $w_{1}(\nu)-\phi^{*}(a)$ , where $a\in H^{1}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is the generator, and this is no data at all; then we also want to impose $w_{2}(\nu)=0$ . So pin $-$ bordism is the Thom spectrum of the twist $f_{a,0}\colon B\mathbb{Z}/2\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{Spin})$ . The classes $a$ and $0$ are $w_{1}$ and $w_{2}$ of $\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , so we learn that $MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\sigma-1}$ , a splitting first written down by Peterson [Pet68, §7].

- (2) A pin $+$ structure is a trivialization of $w_{2}(M)$ , with no condition on $w_{1}$ . Switching to the stable normal bundle, we want a trivialization of $w_{2}(\nu)+w_{1}(\nu)^{2}$ . Just as for pin $-$ structures, pick a map $\phi\colon M\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and ask for a trivialization of $w_{1}(\nu)-\phi^{*}(a)$ , which is no data; then we want to trivialize $w_{2}(\nu)+\phi^{*}(a^{2})$ . Thus pin $+$ bordism is the Thom spectrum of the twist $f_{a,a^{2}}\colon B\mathbb{Z}/2\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{Spin})$ . The classes $a$ and $a^{2}$ are $w_{1}$ , resp. $w_{2}$ of the virtual vector bundle $-\sigma$ , so Lemma 6.18 tells us $MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{1-\sigma}$ , a result of Stolz [Sto88, §8].1212 12 As $[B\mathbb{Z}/2,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{Spin}]$ has exponent $4$ by Example 6.14, $[1-\sigma]=[3\sigma-3]$ , so the reader who prefers to avoid virtual vector bundles can write $MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{3\sigma-3}$ .

- (3) A spin $c$ structure is data of a trivialization of $w_{1}(TM)$ and a class $c_{1}\in H^{2}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ such that $c_{1}\bmod 2=w_{2}(TM)$ ; in this case there is no difference between $w_{2}(TM)$ and $w_{2}(\nu)$ . This is a twisted spin structure where $X=B\mathrm{U}(1)=K(\mathbb{Z},2)$ , $a=0$ , and $b$ is the generator of $H^{2}(K(\mathbb{Z},2);\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ . As $0$ , resp. $b$ are the first and second Stiefel-Whitney classes of the tautological complex line bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , Lemma 6.18 implies $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L-2}$ , which is known due to Bahri-Gilkey [BG87a, BG87b].

- (4) A spin- $\mathbb{Z}/2k$ structure on a manifold $M$ is data of a principal $\mathbb{Z}/k$ -bundle $P\to M$ together with trivializations of $w_{1}(M)$ and $w_{2}(M)-w_{2}(V_{P})$ , where $V$ is the standard one-dimensional complex representation of $\mathbb{Z}/k$ as rotations and $V_{P}\to M$ is the associated complex line bundle to $P$ . Thus, analogous to the spin $c$ argument above, this structure is a twisted spin structure for $X=B\mathbb{Z}/k$ , $a=0$ , and $b=w_{2}(V)$ , and Lemma 6.18 implies $\mathit{MT}\left(\mathrm{Spin}\text{-}\mathbb{Z}/2k\right)\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/k)^{V-2}$ , reproving a theorem of Campbell [Cam17, §7.9].

- (5) A spin $h$ structure is data of a trivialization of $w_{1}(M)$ and a rank- $3$ oriented vector bundle $E\to M$ and a trivialization of $w_{2}(M)-w_{2}(E)$ . Again tangential vs. normal does not matter here, and one can use the same line of reasoning to show that spin $h$ structures are twisted spin structures for $X=B\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ , $a=0$ , and $b=w_{2}$ . As these are $w_{1}$ , resp. $w_{2}$ of the tautological vector bundle $V\to B\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ , Lemma 6.18 tells us $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{h}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SO}_{3})^{V-3}$ , which is due to Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §10].

There are many more examples of vector bundle twists of spin bordism, including the examples in, e.g., [FH21, Guo18, DL20, GOP+20, WW20a, DL21, Ste22, DDHM24]. But one can find twists of spin bordism not described by vector bundle twists, even in physically motivated examples: see [DY24b, Theorem 4.2] for an example where $X=B\mathrm{SU}_{8}/\{\pm 1\}$ , with a few more examples given in [DY23a, §3.1]. The Smith-theoretic techniques in our paper do not apply in those situations.

#### Example 6.24 (James periodicity as Smith periodicity).

James periodicity [Jam59] is a classical result in homotopy theory that the homotopy types of the stunted projective spaces $\mathbb{RP}^{n}_{k}\coloneqq\mathbb{RP}^{n}/\mathbb{RP}^{k}$ (here $k<n$ ) are periodic, with periodicity dependent on $n$ and $k$ . There are also results for the analogously defined stunted complex and quaternionic projective spaces $\mathbb{CP}_{k}^{n}\coloneqq\mathbb{CP}^{n}/\mathbb{CP}^{k}$ and $\mathbb{HP}_{k}^{n}\coloneqq\mathbb{HP}^{n}/\mathbb{HP}^{k}$ . These periodicities can be thought of in terms of periodic Smith families for framed bordism—or conversely, the periodicities in the previous several examples can be thought of as generalizations of James periodicity over other ring spectra than $\mathbb{S}$ .

Proposition 6.10 is the engine behind our periodicity results; its key idea is that vector bundles inducing equivalent maps to $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(R)$ have equivalent $R$ -module Thom spectra. For framed bordism, where $R=\mathbb{S}$ , we therefore should look at the image of the homomorphism $[X,B\mathrm{O}]\to[X,B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})]$ ; following Atiyah [Ati61b, §1], this image is typically denoted $J(X)$ . Atiyah (ibid., Lemma 2.5) proves that if $V,W\to X$ have equal images in $J(X)$ , then $X^{V}\simeq X^{W}$ .1313 13 See Held-Sjerve [HS73, Theorem 1.2] for a partial converse to this result. Therefore we can obtain framed bordism Smith periodicities, or equivalences of Thom spectra, by calculating the groups $J(X)$ . Atiyah (ibid., Proposition 1.5) shows that when $X$ is a finite CW complex, $J(X)$ is a finite group, implying the existence of many framed Smith families.

For James periodicity specifically, choose $F\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C},\mathbb{H}\}$ . Stunted projective spaces are Thom spectra: if $L\to F\mathbb{P}^{k}$ denotes the tautological (real, complex, or quaternionic) line bundle, there is an equivalence $\Sigma^{\infty}F\mathbb{P}_{k}^{n}\simeq(F\mathbb{P}^{k})^{(n-k)L}$ [Ati61b, Proposition 4.3], reducing the proof of James periodicity to the computation of the order of $L$ in $J(F\mathbb{P}^{k})$ . For example, for $F=\mathbb{R}$ Adams calculates the order of $L$ in $J(\mathbb{RP}^{k})$ in [Ada62, Theorem 7.4] and [Ada65a, Example 6.3] to be $2^{\phi(k)}$ , where $\phi(k)$ is the number of integers $s$ with $0<s\leq k$ and $s\equiv 0$ , $1$ , $2$ , or $4\bmod 8$ . Therefore for all $k$ and $n$ , there is a homotopy equivalence

$$ \Sigma^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}_{k}^{n+2^{\phi(k)}}\overset{\simeq}{\longrightarrow}\Sigma^{\infty}\Sigma^{2^{\phi}(k)}\mathbb{RP}_{k}^{n}. $$

(and in fact this is true even before applying $\Sigma^{\infty}$ [Mah65]). Additional computations in $J$ -groups of $F\mathbb{P}^{k}$ are done by Adams-Walker [AW65], Lam [Lam72], Federer-Gitler [FG73, FG77], Sigrist [Sig75], Walker [Wal81], Crabb-Knapp [CK88], Dibağ [Dib99, Dib03], Obiedat [Obi01], and Randal-Williams [RW25, §5.3].

#### Remark 6.26.

There are many other tangential structures $\xi$ that one can study twists of. See [SSS09, Sat10, Sat11a, Sat11b, Sat12, SSS12, Sat15, SW15, SW18, LSW20, SY21, BC22, DY23a] for more examples.

### 6.4. The bound in Proposition 6.10 is not sharp

In this subsection, we discuss ways in which Proposition 6.10 loses information, yielding Smith families with lower-than-expected periodicity. This in particular occurs for twisted string structures.

Proposition 6.10 estimates the periodicity of a Smith family for a tangential structure $\xi$ and vector bundle $V\to X$ in terms of the minimal positive integer $k$ such that $V^{\oplus k}$ has a $\xi$ -structure. As we have seen above in Examples 6.11, 6.12, 6.13, and 6.14, $k$ is finite in many examples of interest, including $\mathrm{O}$ -, $\mathrm{SO}$ -, $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ -, $\mathrm{Spin}$ -, and $\mathrm{U}$ -structures. However, $k$ is not always finite.

#### Lemma 6.27.

- (1) Let $V\to X$ be a real vector bundle whose rational first Pontrjagin class $p_{1}(V)\in H^{4}(X;\mathbb{Q})$ is nonzero. Then for $k\neq 0$ , $V^{\oplus k}$ does not admit a string structure.

- (2) Let $V\to X$ be a complex vector bundle whose rational first Chern class $c_{1}(V)\in H^{2}(X;\mathbb{Q})$ is nonzero. Then for $k\neq 0$ , $V^{\oplus k}$ does not admit an $\mathrm{SU}$ -structure.

#### Proof.

For part (1), if $E\to M$ is a string vector bundle, then $\lambda(E)=0$ implies $p_{1}(E)=0\in H^{4}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ (since $2\lambda=p_{1}$ ), which implies the image of $p_{1}(E)$ in $H^{4}(M;\mathbb{Q})$ is also $0$ , so it suffices to show $p_{1}(V^{\oplus k})$ has nonzero image in $H^{q}(X;\mathbb{Q})$ for $k\neq 0$ . Since $p_{1}(V)$ is nonzero in this group, it is in particular nontorsion, and the Whitney sum formula implies that in $\mathbb{Q}$ -cohomology $p_{1}(V^{\oplus k})=kp_{1}(V)$ , so it is also nonzero. Part (2) is analogous, using that the complete obstruction for lifting from a $\mathrm{U}$ -structure to an $\mathrm{SU}$ -structure is $c_{1}\in H^{2}(B\mathrm{U};\mathbb{Z})$ . ∎

There are many bundles satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 6.27: for example, both are true for the tautological complex line bundle over $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ .

#### Definition 6.28 (Lashof [Las63, §3]).

Let $B\mathrm{U}\langle 6\rangle$ denote the $5$ -connected cover of $B\mathrm{U}$ , and let $\xi\langle 6\rangle\colon B\mathrm{U}\langle 6\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}$ be the composition of the covering map $B\mathrm{U}\langle 6\rangle\to B\mathrm{U}$ and the map $B\mathrm{U}\to B\mathrm{O}$ forgetting the complex structure. We will refer to $\xi\langle 6\rangle$ -structures as $U\langle 6\rangle$ -structures.

A $U\langle 6\rangle$ -structure induces both an $\mathrm{SU}$ -structure and a string structure; the former because the $5$ -connected covering map always factors through the $3$ -connected cover, which for $B\mathrm{U}$ is $B\mathrm{SU}\to B\mathrm{U}$ , and the latter because the map $B\mathrm{U}\langle 6\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}$ must factor through the $5$ -connected cover of $B\mathrm{O}$ , which is $B\mathrm{String}$ .

One can construct two-out-of-three data for $U\langle 6\rangle$ -structures using the $5$ -connected covers of the maps in the two-out-of-three data for $B\mathrm{U}$ . Since this data is constructed in this universal way, it is compatible with the two-out-of-three data we have already used for $\mathrm{U}$ , $\mathrm{SU}$ , $\mathrm{String}$ , etc.

#### Proposition 6.29 (Bauer [Bau03, Lemma 2.1]).

Let $\xi$ be a tangential structure with two-out-of-three data admitting a map $\xi\langle 6\rangle\to\xi$ compatible with two-out-of-three data. If $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ denotes the tautological complex line bundle, then there is a homotopy equivalence

$$ \mathit{MT\xi}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\overset{\simeq}{\longrightarrow}\mathit{MT\xi}\wedge(BU(1))^{24L^{*}-48}. $$

Bauer’s statement in [Bau03, Lemma 2.1] is only a corollary of this, obtained by base-changing from $\mathit{MU}\langle 6\rangle$ to $\mathit{tmf}$ , but in his proof he proves the version we provide here. One can also pass from $L^{*}$ to $L$ by pulling back along the complex conjugation map $B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ .

#### Corollary 6.31.

With $\xi$ as in Proposition 6.29, in particular including string and $\mathrm{SU}$ -structures, every Smith family for $\xi$ -structures and a complex line bundle is at most $24$ -periodic. In particular, Proposition 6.10 is not sharp.

What went wrong? In this specific case, we didn’t use all of the available information in Proposition 6.10. Looking into Bauer’s proof, one learns that the map $[B\mathrm{U}(1),B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}]\to[B\mathrm{U}(1),B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{String})]$ from Theorem 6.7 sends the class of $L^{*}$ , which is infinite-order in $[B\mathrm{U}(1),B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}]$ , to a finite-order class in $[B\mathrm{U}(1),B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(MT\mathrm{String})]$ . Specifically, because this twist came from a vector bundle, it also factors through $[B\mathrm{U}(1),B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}]$ (see Theorem 6.7), and the image of $L^{*}$ in this group has finite order.

#### Proposition 6.32.

For any space $X$ homotopy equivalent to a CW complex with finitely many cells in each degree, let $J_{*}\colon[X,B\mathrm{O}]\to[X,B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}]$ denote the map induced by the $J$ -homomorphism $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ followed by taking the cofiber of $B\mathrm{String}\to B\mathrm{O}\overset{J}{\to}B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ . Then all classes in $\mathrm{Im}(J_{*})$ have finite order.

#### Corollary 6.33.

Every twisted string structure Smith family over a base space $X$ as in Proposition 6.32 has finite periodicity.

#### Proof of Proposition 6.32.

Because $B\mathrm{O}$ and $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ are grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces,1414 14 It is not immediately obvious that $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ is a grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -space, but one can prove it by modifying the argument in [DY23a, Proof of Proposition 1.20]. one can prove the proposition by lifting the map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ to the equivalent data of a map of spectra $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}\colon\mathit{bo}_{0}\to\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/\mathit{bstring}$ .1515 15 The name $\mathit{bo}_{0}$ instead of $\mathit{bo}$ is because it is traditional to use $\mathit{bo}$ to refer to the spectrum corresponding to the grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -space $\mathbb{Z}\times B\mathrm{O}$ , i.e. the spectrum $\mathit{ko}$ .

The map $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}$ was induced from a map of grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces that factored through $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ , and therefore $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}$ factors through $\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ . The homotopy groups of this spectrum are torsion, which follows from May’s definition [May77, §III.2] of $\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ and the triviality of the positive-degree rational stable homotopy groups of the sphere [Ser53]. Thus the rationalization $\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})\wedge H\mathbb{Q}\simeq 0$ . For any class $x\in(\mathit{bo}_{0})^{0}(X)$ , if $J_{*}(x)$ has infinite order, its image in the rationalized $\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/\mathit{bstring}$ -cohomology of $X$ must be nonzero: because $X$ has finitely many cells in each dimension, its generalized cohomology groups for any finite-type spectrum (including all spectra appearing in this proof) are finitely generated, so infinite-order elements persist through rationalization. Rationally, though, $J_{*}$ passes through the zero spectrum. ∎

#### Remark 6.34.

One way to interpret this phenomenon is that, even though the first Pontrjagin class $p_{1}\colon B\mathrm{O}\to K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ descends to a map $p_{1}\colon B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}\to K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ , this map does not extend to a rationally nontrivial map out of $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ . In the language of [DY23a], “a fake vector bundle with respect to twisted string structures has a first Pontrjagin class, but a fake spherical fibration does not.”

#### Remark 6.35 ( $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -families’ periodicity and Bernoulli numbers?).

Propositions 6.32 and 6.33 generalize mutatis mutandis to tangential structures further up the Whitehead tower of $B\mathrm{O}$ . To wit, given a natural number $n$ , let $\xi\colon B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}$ be the $(n-1)$ -connected covering map. This defines a tangential structure commonly called a $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structure, and the two-out-of-three data for $B\mathrm{O}$ pull back by the universal property of the $(n-1)$ -connected cover to define two-out-of-three data for $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures. (Compare Definition 6.28.) Thus Definition 6.1, Example 6.5, and Theorem 6.7 define vector bundle twists, non-vector-bundle twists, and Smith families for twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures just like for string structures.

For $n>4$ , the homotopy groups of $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ are not all torsion, which is downstream from the isomorphism $\pi_{4}(B\mathrm{O})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ [Ste51, §24, §25]. Therefore, like for $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}$ , the order of a twist in $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle]$ is not a particularly good estimate for the value of the corresponding Smith family’s period. Indeed, Propositions 6.32 and 6.33 and their proofs generalize directly from $B\mathrm{String}$ to $B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ , showing all Smith families of twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures have finite order, provided they are over spaces homotopy equivalent to CW complexes with finitely many cells in each dimension. One can also generalize this whole story to the limiting case as $n\to\infty$ , which is the tangential structure $E\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}$ , i.e. a stable framing.

Our proof did not give any estimates on the orders of these Smith families, just finiteness. It would be interesting to bound or compute these orders; for example, one could investigate the map of Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences induced by $j_{/\mathit{bo}\langle n\rangle}$ , the generalization of $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}$ in the proof of Proposition 6.32, or generalize Bauer’s proof in [Bau03, Lemma 2.1]. We suspect that sharp estimates for periodicity for Smith families of twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures will have formulas involving Bernoulli numbers, because of their appearance in Adams’ seminal work computing the image of the $J$ -homomorphism in $\pi_{*}(\mathbb{S})$ [Ada63, Ada65a, Ada65b, Ada66]. We would be interested in learning whether this is the case.

For $n\leq 16$ , twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures as defined here recover familiar twists of familiar tangential structures.

- (0) $\mathrm{O}\langle 0\rangle$ - and $\mathrm{O}\langle 1\rangle$ -structures are canonically equivalent to $\mathrm{O}$ -structures, i.e. no data, and so this story is vacuous.

- (2) $\mathrm{O}\langle 2\rangle$ -structures are equivalent to $\mathrm{SO}$ -structures, and this story recovers the twists in Example 6.19.

- (3) $\pi_{3}(B\mathrm{O})=0$ [Car36, §IV], and $B\mathrm{O}\langle 3\rangle$ and $B\mathrm{O}\langle 4\rangle$ are equivalent to $B\mathrm{Spin}$ . This story recovers the notion of twisted spin structure we discussed in Example 6.23.

- (5) $\pi_{k}(B\mathrm{O})$ vanishes for $k=5$ [Ste51, Remarks 24.11], $k=6$ [Eck51, 3.72], and $k=7$ [BS53, Proposition 19.5], so $B\mathrm{O}\langle 5\rangle$ , $B\mathrm{O}\langle 6\rangle$ , $B\mathrm{O}\langle 7\rangle$ , and $B\mathrm{O}\langle 8\rangle$ all coincide, and are $B\mathrm{String}$ . This story recovers the standard story of twists of string bordism that we mentioned in Example 6.17.

- (9) Sati-Schreiber-Stasheff [SSS09, Definition 1] call an $\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ -structure a fivebrane structure, and in a sequel paper [SSS12, §2.3], they introduce twisted fivebrane structures over a space $X$ given by data of a map $X\to K(\mathbb{Z},8)$ . It is possible to show that their definition is a special case of ours. Specifically, similarly to the identification $K(\mathbb{Z},4)\simeq B\mathrm{Spin}/B\mathrm{String}$ producing a map from the $K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ -twists of string bordism to the more general group of $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}$ twists of string bordism [DY23a, (1.45)], the characteristic class $\tfrac{1}{6}p_{2}\colon B\mathrm{String}\to K(\mathbb{Z},8)$ induces an equivalence of grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces $B\mathrm{String}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle\to K(\mathbb{Z},8)$ , and this equivalence leads to a map $K(\mathbb{Z},8)\simeq B\mathrm{String}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ carrying Sati-Schreiber-Stasheff’s twisted fivebrane structures to a subgroup of the fake vector bundle twists of fivebrane structure.

- (10) Sati [Sat15, Definition 2.4] calls $\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle$ -structures “ $2$ -orientations.” and studies their twists in (ibid., Definition 5.1). Like for twisted fivebrane structures, Sati’s twists are classified by maps to $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,9)\simeq B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ , and map to the twists we considered via the map $B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ .

- (13) As $\pi_{11}(B\mathrm{O})=0$ [Bot59], $\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle$ - and $\mathrm{O}\langle 12\rangle$ -structures coincide. Sati refers to this as a “ $2$ -spin structure” [Sat15, Definition 2.5], and in (ibid., Definition 5.2) introduces twisted $2$ -spin structures corresponding to $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,10)\simeq B\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle$ .

- (14) As $\pi_{k}(B\mathrm{O})=0$ for $k=13$ , $14$ , and $15$ [Bot59], $B\mathrm{O}\langle 13\rangle=\dotsb=B\mathrm{O}\langle 16\rangle$ . Sati [Sat15, Definition 3.1] names this tangential structure a ninebrane structure, and produces twisted ninebrane structures classified by the fractional Pontrjagin class $(1/240)p_{3}\colon B\mathrm{O}\langle 12\rangle\to K(\mathbb{Z},12)$ (ibid., Definition 5.3). As in the previous cases, the map $K(\mathbb{Z},12)\simeq B\mathrm{O}\langle 13\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle$ sends Sati’s twists to ours.

Passing to the infinite limit, we obtain an interpretation of maps to $B\mathrm{O}/E\mathrm{O}$ , i.e. to $B\mathrm{O}$ , as classifying vector bundle twists of framed bordism. These twists of framed bordism are studied in [Cru03, FSS24].

## 7. Examples of Smith fiber sequences

In this section, we implement the discussion from the previous section for some commonly studied vector bundles. We find many previously studied Smith homomorphisms, and also identify a few other well-known cofiber sequences, including Wood’s sequences, Wall’s sequence, and the cofiber sequences associated to the Hopf maps and to transfer maps, as Smith homomorphisms (Examples 7.15 and 7.18). We include this Pokédex of examples in part to illustrate what kinds of Smith cofiber sequences are out there; in part to make contact with preexisting literature; and in part to illustrate how to put theorems such as Theorem 5.1 into practice to explicitly write down Smith cofiber sequences.

### 7.1. Twisting by real line bundles

Our first family of examples use the tautological line bundle $\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ ; its sphere bundle is the tautological $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle $E\mathbb{Z}/2\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , whose total space is contractible. Therefore by Theorem 5.1, for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we have a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{k(\sigma-1)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(k+1)(\sigma-1)}, $$

where $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ is the Smith homomorphism associated to $\sigma$ . When $k=0$ , this is especially nice: the middle spectrum is $\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B\mathbb{Z}/2\simeq\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and the map $\mathbb{S}\to\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma B\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the inclusion of the first factor of the wedge sum, leading to a Smith isomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}\colon\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathbb{Z}/2\overset{\simeq}{\to}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\sigma}$ . This equivalence is well-known; see Kochman [Koc96, Lemma 2.6.5] for a proof.

#### Remark 7.2.

The Thom spectrum $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{k\sigma}$ is often denoted in the homotopy theory literature by $\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}$ , so that $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{k(\sigma-1)}$ can be identified with its desuspension $\Sigma^{-k}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}$ . One justification for this notation stems from (7.1): suspending it $k$ times gives a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}^{k}\longrightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}\longrightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k+1}, $$

which exhibits $\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k+1}$ as the spectrum obtained by crushing the bottom cell of $\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}$ .

#### Example 7.4.

Smash (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{O}$ . As every virtual bundle has a unique $MT\mathrm{O}$ -orientation, this cofiber sequence simplifies to

$$ MT\mathrm{O}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{O}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}MT\mathrm{O}\wedge\Sigma(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

This was the first Smith homomorphism studied; it was defined and named the Smith homomorphism by Conner-Floyd [CF64, Theorem 26.1]. Thom’s celebrated calculation of $\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{O}}$ [Tho54] implies that $MT\mathrm{O}$ is a sum of shifts of $H\mathbb{Z}/2$ ; on each of these copies, the Smith map (7.5) is the cap product with the nonzero element of $H^{1}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ .

Stong [Sto69, Proposition 5] and Uchida [Uch70] study related examples, where one smashes (7.5) with spaces $X$ ; they identify the fiber $MT\mathrm{O}\wedge X$ and show that the long exact sequence of homotopy groups splits. Their papers are among the earliest examples identifying the Smith long exact sequence.1616 16 At the time, it was common to think of $\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{O}}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)$ as the bordism groups of manifolds $M$ equipped with a free involution $\tau$ , rather than manifolds with a principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle; Stong and Uchida’s results are phrased in that language. To pass between these perspectives, rewrite $(M,\tau)$ as the principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle $M\to M/\tau$ ; in the other direction, take the deck transformation involution of the total space of a principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle.

#### Example 7.6.

Smash (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{SO}$ . Since $\sigma$ is not orientable, but $2\sigma$ is oriented (see Example 6.12), we obtain a $2$ -periodic series of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms between the oriented bordism of $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted oriented bordism. The latter can be identified with unoriented bordism: a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted orientation on $V$ is data of a line bundle on $L$ and an orientation of $V\oplus L$ , which is no data at all: this identifies $L\cong\mathrm{Det}(V)^{\ast}\cong\mathrm{Det}(V)$ up to a contractible space of choices, and $V\oplus\mathrm{Det}(V)$ is canonically oriented. So every vector bundle has a canonical $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted orientation.

Therefore by Theorem 5.1 we obtain a $2$ -periodic sequence of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms:

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{SO}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{O} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{SO}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{O}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

These maps are obtained by taking smooth representatives of Poincaré duals of $w_{1}$ either of the manifold (when the domain is $\Omega_{\ast}^{\mathrm{O}}$ ) or of the principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle (when the domain is $\Omega_{\ast}^{\mathrm{SO}}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)$ ). See [DDK+25, §IV.B] for the physical interpretation of the corresponding long exact sequence of Anderson dual groups.

These Smith homomorphisms were first introduced by Komiya [Kom72, §5]; see also Shibata [Shi73, Proposition 2.1]. See Córdova-Ohmori-Shao-Yan [COSY20, Appendix A], Hason-Komargodski-Thorngren [HKT20, §4.4], and Fidkowski-Haah-Hastings [FHH20] for applications of these Smith homomorphisms to physics. The splitting of the $k=0$ case of (7.1) implies a homotopy equivalence $MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{\cong}\Sigma MT\mathrm{O}$ , a theorem of Atiyah [Ati61a, Proposition 4.1].

#### Example 7.8.

Some of the coolest examples of this kind come about by smashing (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ . As we discussed in Example 6.14, the periodicity of this family is $1$ , $2$ , or $4$ ; a Whitney sum formula calculation shows that $k\sigma$ is spin iff $k$ is a multiple of $4$ , and therefore this Smith family is $4$ -periodic. The corresponding $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted spin bordism groups can be identified with $H$ -bordism for certain Lie groups $H$ , as discussed in Example 6.23; specifically,

- (1) a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent to a pin $-$ structure;

- (2) a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,2\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent to an $H$ structure, where $H=\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ ; and

- (3) a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,3\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent to a pin $+$ structure.

Using Theorem 5.1 once again, the $4$ -periodic sequence of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms takes the form

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4) \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}, $$

with each $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ obtained by taking a smooth representative of a Poincaré dual of $w_{1}$ of the manifold or of a associated principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle, like in (7.7).

The splitting of the $k=0$ Smith homomorphism in (7.1) gives us an equivalence $MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2\simeq MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-}$ , a theorem of Peterson [Pet68, §7].

This family of Smith homomorphisms has been discussed in the literature before. The piece involving $\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathrm{Pin}^{-}$ was used by Peterson [Pet68, §7] and Anderson-Brown-Peterson [ABP69], who say that it was already “well-known.” The long exact sequence corresponding to (7.9c) appears in [Gia73b, Theorem 3.1], where it is attributed to Stong. The Smith homomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ in (7.9d) appears in Kreck [Kre84, §4]. The long exact sequence induced by (7.9b) is used by Botvinnik-Rosenberg [BR23, §2], who also discuss (7.9c) and (7.9d). The composition of two maps in (7.9) in a row to go between pin $+$ and pin $-$ bordism appears in Kirby-Taylor [KT90a, Lemma 7]. We work out the corresponding long exact sequences, as well as some physical consequences for all four Smith homomorphisms in [DDK+25, §IV.C].

The full family appears more recently in work of Hambleton-Su [HS13, §4.C], Kapustin-Thorngren-Turzillo-Wang [KTTW15, §8], Tachikawa-Yonekura [TY19, §3.1], Hason-Komargodski-Thorngren [HKT20, §4.4], and Wan-Wang-Zheng [WWZ20, §6.7]. Ekholm [Ekh98] produces the $4$ -periodic sequence of tangential structures in a different setting but does not discuss the Smith homomorphism.

#### Example 7.10.

As we discussed in Example 6.17, for a general vector bundle $V\to X$ , there is no guarantee that $kV$ has a string structure. However, on $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , $k\sigma$ has a string structure iff $k\equiv 0\bmod 8$ , so there is an eight-periodic family of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms between bordism groups of manifolds with $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted string structures for various $k$ .1717 17 To prove the claimed fact about string structures on $k\sigma$ , first use the Whitney sum formula to show that $w_{1}(k\sigma)$ , $w_{2}(k\sigma)$ , and $w_{4}(k\sigma)$ all vanish iff $k\equiv 0\bmod 8$ . The reduction mod $2$ map $H^{4}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z})\to H^{4}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is an isomorphism, so the string obstruction $\lambda(k\sigma)$ vanishes iff its mod $2$ reduction does, and $\lambda\bmod 2=w_{4}$ .

In Example 7.8, each $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure for $k\in\mathbb{Z}/4$ turned out to be equivalent to a $G[k]$ -structure for four Lie groups $G[k]$ : $G[0]\cong\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ , $G[1]\cong\mathrm{Pin}^{-}$ , $G[2]\cong\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ , and $G[3]\cong\mathrm{Pin}^{+}$ (see also [TY19, (3.1)]). An analogous result is true for the eight twisted string structures, but in the world of $2$ -groups, because the string group is a Lie $2$ -group [SP11]. We will see that for each $k\in\mathbb{Z}/8$ , there is a Lie $2$ -group $\mathbb{G}[k]$ and a map $\xi\colon B\mathbb{G}[k]\to B\mathrm{O}$ such that $\mathbb{G}[k]$ -structures on a smooth manifolds are naturally equivalent to $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted string structures. Though it is difficult to describe $\mathbb{G}[k]$ explicitly for most $k$ , we will realize it as an extension of $G[k\bmod 4]$ by $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ : such extensions of a compact Lie group $G$ by $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ are classified by $H^{4}(BG;\mathbb{Z})$ [SP11, Wei22], and we will find classes in this cohomology group classifying all eight $\mathbb{G}[k]$ $2$ -groups.

Recall from Example 6.23 that if $V\to X$ is a pin $\pm$ vector bundle, then $V\mp\mathrm{Det}(V)$ has a canonical spin structure, meaning that the string obstruction class $\lambda(V\mp\mathrm{Det}(V))\in H^{4}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is defined. Let

$$ \lambda^{\pm}\coloneqq\lambda(V\mp\mathrm{Det}(V))\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{Pin}^{\pm};\mathbb{Z}). $$

The inclusion $j\colon\mathbb{Z}/2\hookrightarrow\mathrm{U}(1)$ pulls back the tautological complex line bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ to $2\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Therefore a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,2\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure induces a $(B\mathrm{U}(1),L)$ -twisted spin structure—or in the language of Example 6.23, a $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ structure induces a spin $c$ structure via $j$ . Let $\lambda^{c}\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{Spin}^{c};\mathbb{Z})$ be the class defined in [DY24a, Definition 2.6],1818 18 The class $\lambda^{c}$ is called $q_{2}$ in [Dua18] and $\widehat{p}_{2}$ in [CN19, §2.7]. In the notation of [CY20, (3.10)], $\lambda^{c}=c_{1}(L)^{2}-p_{c}$ , and in [Dev22, Construction 2], $\lambda^{c}=c_{1}(L)^{2}-(c_{1}^{2}-p_{1})/2$ , where $L$ is the determinant line bundle. namely $\lambda(V\oplus L)$ , where $L$ is the determinant bundle of the spin $c$ structure. Pulling back by $j$ , we will regard $\lambda^{c}$ as a class in $H^{4}(B(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4);\mathbb{Z}/2)$ .

Thus, essentially by definition, for $k=-1,0,1,2\bmod 8$ , the obstruction to lifting from a $G[k\bmod 4]$ -structure to a $\mathbb{G}[k]$ -structure is respectively $\lambda^{+}(V)$ , $\lambda(V)$ , $\lambda^{-}(V)$ , and $\lambda^{c}(V)$ , where $V\to BG[k]$ is the tautological bundle. This gives the first half of Table 1.

Let $e^{\mathbb{Z}}\in H^{1}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}_{w_{1}(\sigma)})$ denote the twisted $\mathbb{Z}$ -cohomology Euler class as defined in Definition 4.4 for $\mathcal{R}=H\mathbb{Z}$ . Čadek [Čad99, Lemma 1] shows that $(e^{\mathbb{Z}})^{2\ell}$ is an untwisted class, and moreover is the unique nonzero element of $H^{2\ell}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z})$ . Thus, since $4\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ is spin but not string (see Footnote 17), the class $\lambda(4\sigma)$ is defined and equals $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(\sigma)^{4}$ . The string obstruction $\lambda$ satisfies a Whitney sum formula [Deb24, Lemma 1.6] for pairs of spin vector bundles,1919 19 See also Johnson-Freyd and Treumann [JFT20, §1.4] for a proof sketch and Jenquin [Jen05, Corollary 4.9] for a similar result in a generalized cohomology theory. so for $k=3,4,5,6\bmod 8$ ,

$$ \lambda(V+k\sigma)=\lambda(V+(k-4)\sigma)+\lambda(4\sigma)=\lambda(V+(k-4)\sigma)+e^{\mathbb{Z}}(\sigma)^{4}, $$

so by adding $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(\sigma)^{4}$ to the obstruction classes for the first four entries in Table 1, we get the obstruction classes for the remaining entries.

In some cases it is possible to describe $\mathbb{G}[k]$ more explicitly. For example, when $k\equiv 0\bmod 8$ , we get $\mathbb{G}[0]=\mathrm{String}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ , as the obstruction class is trivial on the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ factor. When $k\equiv 4\bmod 8$ , $\mathbb{G}[4]=\mathrm{String}\times_{B\mathrm{U}(1)}\mathsf{sLine}$ , where $\mathsf{sLine}$ is the abelian Lie $2$ -group of Hermitian super lines. This can be proven in a similar manner to [DDHM24, Corollary 10.23], which establishes an analogous result for twisted spin structures. Here we use that $\mathsf{sLine}$ is the extension of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ by $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ classified by $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(\sigma)^{4}$ ; since $H^{4}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ , this follows as soon as we know that $\mathsf{sLine}$ is a nonsplit central extension of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ , which is straightforward.

#### Example 7.13.

If one smashes (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , one obtains a very similar story to Example 7.6: twice any vector bundle is complex, hence spin $c$ , and $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted spin $c$ bordism is naturally identified with pin $c$ bordism, as we discussed in Example 6.21. So taking Poincaré duals of $w_{1}$ as in Example 7.6 defines a $2$ -periodic sequence of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

To our knowledge, these long exact sequences first appear in Hambleton-Su [HS13, §4.C].

We also obtain an equivalence $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2\overset{\simeq}{\to}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c}$ , which was first observed by Bahri-Gilkey [BG87a, §3]. See Shiozaki-Shapourian-Ryu [SSR17, §E.1] and Kobayashi [Kob21, §IV] for applications in condensed-matter physics and [DYY25a] for an application of a closely related Smith long exact sequence.

#### Example 7.15.

Pull back (7.1) along the map $B\mathbb{Z}\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , i.e. $S^{1}=\mathbb{RP}^{1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}$ . The sphere bundle of $\sigma\to\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ is not contractible: it is the double cover $S^{1}\to\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ , and its Thom space is $\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ . Therefore we obtain from Theorem 5.1 a cofiber sequence $\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}S^{1}\to\Sigma^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}\to\Sigma_{+}^{1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ , which is a rotated version of the multiplication-by- $2$ cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}\overset{2}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{-1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}. $$

The same story applies to the complex, quaternionic, and octonionic Hopf fibrations: their cofibers are the respective projective planes $\Sigma^{-2+\infty}\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ , $\Sigma^{-4+\infty}\mathbb{HP}^{2}$ , and $\Sigma^{-8+\infty}\mathbb{OP}^{2}$ , and in each case the map to the cofiber is a Smith homomorphism for the tautological line bundle over the respective projective line (which is a sphere). In the case of the complex Hopf fibration, after smashing with $\mathit{ko}$ or $\mathit{KO}$ , one obtains the Wood cofiber sequences [Woo63] $\Sigma\mathit{KO}\xrightarrow{\eta}\mathit{KO}\to\mathit{KU}$ and $\Sigma\mathit{ko}\xrightarrow{\eta}\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{ku}$ as rotated versions of Smith cofiber sequences.

Smash (7.16) with $MT\mathrm{SO}$ and you obtain Wall’s cofiber sequence [Wal60, Theorem 3]

$$ MT\mathrm{SO}\overset{2}{\longrightarrow}MT\mathrm{SO}\longrightarrow\mathcal{W}, $$

where $\mathcal{W}$ is the Thom spectrum whose homotopy groups are the bordism groups of manifolds with an integral lift of $w_{1}$ . This follows from Atiyah’s identification of $\mathcal{W}\simeq\Sigma^{-1}MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ [Ati61a, §4], but it is also easy to directly check that an integral lift of $w_{1}$ is equivalent data to a $(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)$ -twisted orientation, using that $\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ is a $B\mathbb{Z}$ .

It is also interesting to smash (7.16) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ ; we work out the induced long exact sequence of bordism groups in low degrees in Figure 2, and this long exact sequence also appears in [DYY25a].

#### Example 7.18.

Let $\pi\colon E\to B$ be a principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle and $L\coloneqq E\times_{\mathbb{Z}/2}\mathbb{R}\to B$ be the associated line bundle. Then we have a Smith homomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{L}\colon B^{-L}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B$ . The fiber is the Thom spectrum of the pullback of $L$ to its sphere bundle; the sphere bundle is $E$ and $\pi^{\ast}(L)$ is trivial, so Theorem 5.1 gives us a cofiber sequence

$$ B^{-L}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B\overset{\tau}{\longrightarrow}\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}E. $$

#### Lemma 7.20.

The map $\tau$ in (7.19) is the Becker-Gottlieb transfer [Rou72, KP72, BG75] for $\pi$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to work universally with the Smith cofiber sequence $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{-\sigma}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B\mathbb{Z}/2\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}E\mathbb{Z}/2$ , i.e. $(\mathbb{RP}^{\infty})^{-\sigma}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}\to\mathbb{S}$ , and to show that the latter map is the transfer for $E\mathbb{Z}/2\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ .

This transfer map admits the following description: consider the map of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -spectra2020 20 This fact, and our argument using it, works for both Borel and genuine $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -spectra. $f\colon\mathbb{S}\to\Sigma^{1-\sigma}(\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}$ , whose cofiber is $\mathbb{S}^{-\sigma}$ . Upon taking homotopy orbits, we obtain a map $f_{h\mathbb{Z}/2}\colon\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}\to\mathbb{S}$ , and this is the transfer map.

If $G$ is a finite group and $V\in\mathit{RO}(G)$ , there is a natural equivalence of spectra $(\mathbb{S}^{V})_{hG}\simeq(BG)^{V}$ .2121 21 One quick way to prove this uses the Ando-Blumberg-Gepner-Hopkins-Rezk approach to Thom spectra [ABG+14a, ABG+14b]: both $(\mathbb{S}^{V})_{hG}$ and $(BG)^{V}$ are both the colimit of the $\mathrm{pt}/G$ -shaped diagram whose value on $\mathrm{pt}$ is $\mathbb{S}^{V}$ and whose value on the morphism set $G$ encodes the $G$ -action on $\mathbb{S}^{V}$ [ABG+14a, Theorem 1.17]. It is also possible to prove this more classically by working with Thom spaces. And taking homotopy orbits of $G$ -spectra preserves cofiber sequences, so the fiber of the transfer $f_{h\mathbb{Z}/2}$ is the map $(\mathbb{RP}^{\infty})^{-\sigma}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}$ given by the “inclusion” of virtual representations $-\sigma\hookrightarrow 0$ , which is the Smith homomorphism we began with. ∎

In the case that $B$ is a finite CW complex, one can prove Lemma 7.20 more classically by adapting Cusick’s calculation [Cus85, Corollary 2.11] identifying the cofibers of transfer maps for double covers.

#### Remark 7.21.

For another example along the lines of (7.19), Morisugi [Mor09, Theorem 1.3] shows that the cofibers of certain Smith homomorphisms over compact Lie groups can be described as Becker-Schultz transfer maps [BS74, §4]. And Uchida [Uch69], motivated by the study of immersions, works out the Smith long exact sequences of a few special cases of Example 7.18, where $E=B\mathrm{O}(k)\times B\mathrm{O}(k)$ and $B=B(\mathrm{O}(1)\ltimes(\mathrm{O}(k)^{\times 2}))$ , where $\mathrm{O}(1)$ acts on $\mathrm{O}(k)^{\times 2}$ by swapping the two factors.

#### Remark 7.22.

The ease of modifying the Smith long exact sequence by a vector bundle twist suggests that Example 7.18 could be generalized to some sort of twisted transfer map. The relevant twisted transfer maps have been constructed by Kashiwabara-Zare [KZ18].

### 7.2. Twisting by complex line bundles

Now we consider the analogous family of examples arising from the tautological complex line bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ . Its sphere bundle is $E\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , which is contractible, so just like in (7.1), we have for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{k(L-2)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{(k+1)(L-2)}. $$

Again, when $k=0$ , this sequence splits, yielding another Smith isomorphism $\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathrm{U}(1)\xrightarrow{\cong}(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L}$ . This equivalence is well-known, e.g. [Ada74, Example 2.1].

#### Example 7.24.

Let $G$ be one of $\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , or $\mathrm{U}$ ; then the tautological line bundle over $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ has a $G$ -structure, and $\mathit{MTG}$ is an $E_{\infty}$ -ring spectrum and we can make sense of $G$ -orientations. The $G$ -orientation on $L$ untwists the Thom spectrum, so smashing (7.23) with $\mathit{MTG}$ has a similar effect to Example 7.4: the result is a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathit{MTG}\longrightarrow\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}. $$

For $G=\mathrm{U}$ , this Smith homomorphism was first studied by Conner-Floyd [CF66b, §5], and also appears in Ray [Ray72, §3].

#### Lemma 7.26.

For $G=\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , or $\mathrm{U}$ , there is an $\mathit{MTG}$ -module equivalence

$$ \mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\simeq\bigvee_{k\geq 0}\Sigma^{2k}\mathit{MTG}. $$

#### Proof.

The zeroth step is splitting off the basepoint: $\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\simeq\mathit{MTG}\vee\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))$ . As noted above, $\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathrm{U}(1)\simeq(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L}$ , and we have a Thom isomorphism $\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L}\simeq\mathit{MTG}\wedge\Sigma^{2}(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}$ of $\mathit{MTG}$ -modules. We are now in the same situation as at the beginning of the proof, but shifted up by $2$ , and we carry on in a similar way. ∎

#### Example 7.28.

Smash (7.23) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ ; the bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ is oriented but not spin, so $2L$ is spin, and therefore we obtain a $2$ -periodic, codimension- $2$ family of Smith homomorphisms between the spin bordism of $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ and $(B\mathrm{U}(1),L)$ -twisted spin bordism. A $(B\mathrm{U}(1),L)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent data to a spin $c$ structure, as we discussed in Example 6.23, so this Smith family takes the form

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}. $$

The long exact sequence arising from (7.29a) was identified by Kirby-Taylor [KT90b, Corollary 6.12, Remark 6.14]. The splitting of (7.23) when $k=0$ leads to an equivalence $MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge B\mathrm{U}(1)\simeq\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , a theorem due to Stong [Sto68, Chapter XI]. We discuss the physical interpretation of (7.29) in [DDK+25, §IV.A].

It would be interesting to study analogues of this example for pin $c$ or pin $\tilde{c}\pm$ bordism and applications to invertible phases. Kirby-Taylor [KT90b, Remark 6.15] consider two additional analogues of (7.29a), one of which is related to a Smith long exact sequence for $G$ -bordism where $G\coloneqq\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathrm{O}(2)$ (see [DYY25b, §3.3]). Stehouwer [Ste22, §4] computes $G$ -bordism groups in low dimensions, and $G$ -bordism also appears in [DDHM22, DDHM24, DYY25a]. In addition, Hambleton-Kreck-Teichner [HKT94, §2] study a pin $-$ and pin $c$ analogue of Example 7.28.
