As noted above, $S(L)$ is contractible as it is the total space of the universal fibration. Therefore, the other three corners of the square form a fiber sequence. To compute the fiber of $B\mathbb{Z}/n\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , we notice that applying the classifying space functor to the short exact sequence $\mathbb{Z}/n\hookrightarrow\mathrm{U}(1)\xrightarrow{\times n}\mathrm{U}(1)$ gives a fibration $B\mathbb{Z}/n\to B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ . Then, recognizing the map $B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ as the classifying map for a principal $\mathrm{U}(1)$ -bundle over $\mathrm{U}(1)$ with total space $B\mathbb{Z}/n$ , we conclude that the fiber of the map $B\mathbb{Z}/n\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ is exactly $\mathrm{U}(1)$ . So, $S(i^{*}L)\simeq S^{1}$ .

Next, we need to pull back $V_{1}$ along the projection $p\colon S(i^{*}L)\to B\mathbb{Z}/n$ . We have that $p^{*}(k(i^{*}L-1))\cong\bigoplus_{k}p^{*}(i^{*}L)$ . Since $L$ is oriented as a real vector bundle, its pullbacks are as well, so $p^{*}i^{*}L$ is oriented when considered as a real vector bundle over $S^{1}$ , and thus it is the trivial 2-plane bundle.

Therefore, we recognize the Thom spectrum $S(i^{*}L)^{kp^{*}(i^{*}L)}$ as

$$ \displaystyle S(i^{*}L)^{kp^{*}(i^{*}L)} \displaystyle\simeq(S^{1})^{k} \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k}\textnormal{Th}(S^{1};0) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k}(\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}S^{1}) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k}(\Sigma^{\infty}S^{1}\oplus\Sigma^{\infty}S^{0}) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k+1}\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma^{2k}\mathbb{S}. $$

Thus for each $k\geq 0$ we have a Smith cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma^{2k+1}\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma^{2k}\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/n)^{k\cdot i^{*}L}\longrightarrow B\mathbb{Z}/n^{(k+1)i^{*}L}. $$

Finally, we place $V_{1}$ in virtual dimension zero by taking $V_{1}=k(i^{*}L-2)$ , to be consistent with the other examples in this section, and obtain the cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma\mathbb{S}\vee\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/n)^{k(i^{*}L-2)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}(B\mathbb{Z}/n)^{(k+1)(i^{*}L-2)}. $$

#### Example 7.35.

Smash (7.34) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ . Like in Example 7.28, $i^{*}L$ is oriented but not spin, and $2i^{*}L$ is spin, so we obtain a $2$ -periodic, codimension- $2$ family of Smith homomorphisms between the spin bordism of $B\mathbb{Z}/n$ and $(B\mathbb{Z}/n,i^{*}L)$ -twisted spin bordism. Campbell [Cam17, §7.9] identifies the latter as bordism for the tangential structure $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2n$ , explicitly giving us Smith cofiber sequences

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\vee MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2k)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{i^{*}L}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/k)_{+} \displaystyle\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\vee MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/k)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{i^{*}L}}\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2k). $$

$\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2k$ bordism appears in the mathematical physics literature in [Bel99, Bla00, BBC17, Cam17, GEM19, Hsi18, Jan18, Li19, GOP+20, DDHM22, Deb21, DL21, DDHM24, HTY22, DYY25a]; the case $k=2$ also appears in [Gia73a, TY19, FH20, HKT20, MV21]. The Smith homomorphisms in (7.36) for $n=4$ appear in [DDHM24]. We work out the Anderson-dualized long exact sequences corresponding to (7.36) for the $n=3$ case in [DDK+25, §IV.D], and for the $n=4$ case in [DDK+25, §IV.E].

#### Example 7.37.

We elaborate on Example 7.35 when $n=2$ . The rotation representation is isomorphic to $2\sigma$ , where $\sigma$ denotes the real sign representation; we will also let $\sigma$ denote the associated bundle over $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ .

Everything in Example 7.35 still works for $n=2$ , but now we have more options: we can start with an odd number of copies of $\sigma$ . In this case, the fiber of the Smith map is the Thom spectrum of the Möbius bundle $(\sigma-1)\to\mathrm{U}(1)$ ; one can directly check that the Thom space of $\sigma$ is $\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ , so the Thom spectrum of $\sigma-1$ is $\Sigma^{-1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ . Therefore we have a Smith cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma^{-1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(2k-1)(\sigma-1)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}}\Sigma^{2}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(2k+1)(\sigma-1)}. $$

Out of all the examples we have studied in this section, this is the first one where the pullback of $V$ to the sphere bundle of $W$ is nontrivial.

As usual, we smash (7.38) with various bordism spectra. The map $\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}$ is the composition of two iterations of $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ from (7.1), so some of the resulting cofiber sequences look familiar from that perspective. We only discuss a few examples, but plenty more are out there.

- • If we smash (7.38) with $MT\mathrm{SO}$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence first discussed by Atiyah [Ati61a, (4.3)]: (7.39)

$$ \mathcal{W}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{O}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{O}, $$

where $\mathcal{W}$ is Wall’s bordism spectrum (see Example 7.15). Here we use the identifications $\Sigma MT\mathrm{O}\simeq MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathcal{W}\simeq MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ , both due to Atiyah [Ati61a, §4], that we discussed in Examples 7.15 and 7.6, respectively.

- • If we instead smash (7.38) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence (7.40)

$$ MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb{RP}^{2}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{\pm}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Pin}^{\mp}, $$

which was first constructed by Kirby-Taylor [KT90a, Lemma 7]. Here we have used the identifications of pin $+$ , resp. pin $-$ bordism as $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,3\sigma)$ , resp. $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted spin bordism that we discussed in Example 7.8. In Figure 3, we calculate the long exact sequence on bordism groups corresponding to (7.40) (specifically, the pin $-$ to pin $+$ case) in low degrees. See [DDHM24] for an application of a related but different Smith homomorphism in physics. The Smith homomorphism in (7.40) is the composition of two of the Smith homomorphisms in the $4$ -periodic collection of Example 7.8, where we go from pin $+$ to $\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ to pin $-$ , or from pin $-$ to $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ to pin $+$ . The other two compositions, which exchange the spin bordism of $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ with $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ bordism, are (7.36) for $n=2$ .

### 7.3. A few more examples

In this section, we record some examples of Smith cofiber sequences that do not arise from real or complex line bundles.

#### Example 7.41.

Like our previous examples over $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , we can study Smith homomorphisms for the tautological quaternionic line bundle $V\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . Once again, the sphere bundle of $V$ is contractible, as it is $E\mathrm{SU}(2)\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ , so we obtain Smith cofiber sequences like in (7.1) and (7.23):

$$ \mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{k(V-4)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{4}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{(k+1)(V-4)}. $$

For $k=0$ , this sequence splits, yielding a third Smith isomorphism $\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathrm{SU}(2)\xrightarrow{\cong}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{V}$ . This equivalence is well-known, e.g. [Tam97, §2].

This bundle has a $G$ -structure for $G$ including $\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , $\mathrm{U}$ , $\mathrm{SU}$ , and $\mathrm{Sp}$ , and in all of these cases, smashing with $\mathit{MTG}$ produces Smith homomorphisms similar to those in Examples 7.4 and 7.24. The proof of Lemma 7.26 still works in this setting, and for these $G$ we obtain $\mathit{MTG}$ -module splittings

$$ \mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))_{+}\simeq\bigvee_{k\geq 0}\Sigma^{4k}\mathit{MTG}. $$

When $G=\mathrm{Spin}$ , (7.43) is closely related to the splittings in Lemmas B.13 and B.15.

The Smith map (7.42), after smashing with $\mathit{MTSp}$ , was studied by Landweber [Lan68, §5] and Ray [Ray72, §3]. An analogue in self-conjugate bordism (see [SS68, §8]) was studied by Gozman [Goz77, §3].

#### Example 7.44.

As we mentioned in Example 7.10, Lie $2$ -group extensions of a compact Lie group $G$ by $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ are classified by $H^{4}(BG;\mathbb{Z})$ [SP11, Wei22]. Let $\mathrm{String}\text{-}\mathrm{SU}(2)$ be the Lie $2$ -group belonging to the extension

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B\mathrm{U}(1)}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{String}\text{-}\mathrm{SU}(2)}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{0}} $$

classified by $\lambda+p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{Spin}\times B\mathrm{SU}(2);\mathbb{Z})$ ; here $\lambda\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{Spin};\mathbb{Z})$ and $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{SU}(2);\mathbb{Z})$ are the canonical generators of $H^{4}$ of a connected, simply connected, simple Lie group. (For $B\mathrm{Spin}$ , we may use $B\mathrm{Spin}(n)$ with $n\gg 0$ .) Using the usual map $\mathrm{Spin}\to\mathrm{O}$ , we obtain a tangential structure $B(\mathrm{String}\text{-}\mathrm{SU}(2))\to B\mathrm{O}$ ; by an argument similar to the one in [DDHM24, §10.4] (see [BDDM24, §3.3.1]), $\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{String}\text{-}\mathrm{SU}(2))\simeq MT\mathrm{String}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{L-4}$ , where $L\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is the tautological quaternionic line bundle. Thus (7.42) with $k=0$ , smashed with $MT\mathrm{String}$ , produces a Smith isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{sm}_{L}\colon\widetilde{\Omega}_{*}^{\mathrm{String}}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))\overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow}\Omega_{*-4}^{\mathrm{String}\text{-}\mathrm{SU}(2)}. $$

As $L\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is not string, the argument for (7.43) does not apply, and indeed one can show $\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{String}\text{-}\mathrm{SU}(2))$ does not split in that way. Thus this Smith isomorphism is expressing something nontrivial about string- $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ bordism. To our knowledge, (7.46) is the first such nontrivial quaternionic Smith isomorphism known.

String- $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ bordism appears in [BDDM24, §3] as an intermediary to other twisted string bordism computations, and Bruner-Rognes [BR21, §1.4, Chapter 8, §12.3, Appendix D] study a closely related object called $\mathit{tmf}/\nu$ .

#### Example 7.47.

Consider the Smith homomorphisms coming from the tautological rank- $3$ vector bundle $V\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ . The one-point compactification of $\mathfrak{so}(3)/\mathfrak{u}_{1}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{U}(1)\cong S^{2}$ . Since $\mathfrak{so}(3)/\mathfrak{u}_{1}\oplus\mathbb{R}$ is isomorphic to the defining representation $V$ of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence of spectra

$$ (B\mathrm{U}(1))^{k(L-2)}\longrightarrow(B\mathrm{SO}(3))^{k(V-3)}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{3}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))^{(k+1)(V-3)}. $$

We are most interested in smashing this sequence with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ .2222 22 It is also interesting to smash (7.48) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ : in this case one obtains a codimension- $3$ , $2$ -periodic family of Smith homomorphisms exchanging the spin $c$ bordism of $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ with “spin- $\mathrm{U}(2)$ bordism,” i.e. bordism of the group $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathrm{U}(2)\cong\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . Davighi-Lohitsiri [DL20, DL21] introduced Spin- $\mathrm{U}(2)$ bordism and calculated it in low dimensions; spin- $\mathrm{U}(2)$ structures also appear in Seiberg-Witten theory (e.g. [FL02, DW19]) under the name spin $u$ structures. Note that $V$ is not spin, but because $V$ is oriented, $2V$ is spin; therefore we obtain a $2$ -periodic family of codimension- $3$ Smith homomorphisms exchanging the spin bordism of $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $(B\mathrm{SO}(3),V)$ -twisted spin bordism. Freed-Hopkins [FH21, (10.20)] identify $(B\mathrm{SO}(3),V)$ -twisted spin bordism with bordism for the group $G^{0}\coloneqq\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathrm{SU}(2)$ , which is in various sources called spin $h$ bordism, spin $q$ bordism, spin- $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ bordism, or $G^{0}$ bordism.2323 23 To the best of our knowledge, spin $h$ structures were first studied in [BFF78] in the context of quantum gravity; they have also been applied to Seiberg-Witten theory [OT96], index theory, e.g. in [May65, Nag95, Bär99, FH21, Che17], almost quaternionic geometry, e.g. in [Nag95, Bär99, AM21], immersion problems [Bär99, AM21], and the study of invertible field theories [FH21, BC18, WWW19, DY24b]. See [Law23] for a review and [BM23, Hu23, Mil24, DK25] for additional related work. The fiber we’ve seen before in Example 7.28: spin $c$ bordism when $k$ is odd in (7.48), and the spin bordism of $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ when $k$ is even.

In summary, we have two Smith cofiber sequences

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}^{h}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{3}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SO}(3))_{+} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SO}(3))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{3}MT\mathrm{Spin}^{h}. $$

The long exact sequence of bordism groups associated to (7.49a) appears in Theorem B.2 as an example where one must use the cobordism Euler class to calculate the Smith homomorphism: ordinary cohomology Euler classes give the wrong answer. Other works studying anomalies of spin $h$ QFTs include [FH21, WW19, WWW19, WWZ20, DL20, WW20b, BCD22, DY24b, WY22, DYY25a].

#### Remark 7.50.

Freed-Hopkins [FH21] also study two unoriented analogues of spin $h$ structures, called pin $h\pm$ or $G^{\pm}$ structures, corresponding to the groups $\mathrm{Pin}^{\pm}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . It would be interesting to work out analogues of the Smith homomorphisms such as the ones in Examples 7.8 and 7.47 for pin $h\pm$ structures and apply them to symmetry breaking; see [DK25] for some work in that direction. Pin $h\pm$ manifolds are also studied in [BC18, GPW18, LS19, AM21, DYY25a].

#### Example 7.51.

If we pull Example 7.47 back to $B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ , we obtain a Smith long exact sequence which makes an appearance both in [DDK+25, §IV.F] and in Appendix B.

The tautological quaternionic line bundle over $B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is not isomorphic to the bundle associated to $\mathfrak{su}_{2}\oplus\mathbb{R}$ , where $\mathfrak{su}_{2}$ is the adjoint representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . Rather, since $\mathfrak{su}_{2}\cong\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathfrak{su}_{2}/\mathfrak{u}_{1}$ , the map $B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ exhibits $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ as the unit sphere bundle in the adjoint representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . It follows that there is a cofiber sequence

$$ B\mathrm{U}(1)\longrightarrow B\mathrm{SU}(2)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{3}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{V-3}, $$

where $V\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is the vector bundle associated to $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ . We claim the first map is induced by the inclusion of a maximal torus into $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . To see that the sphere bundle is $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ as claimed, identify $\mathrm{SU}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ with $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathrm{U}(1)\to\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with $\mathrm{Spin}(2)\to\mathrm{Spin}(3)$ ; by the third isomorphism theorem, $\mathrm{Spin}(3)/\mathrm{Spin}(2)\cong\mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{SO}(2)$ , and in Example 7.47 we identified that quotient with the unit sphere inside $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Therefore taking associated bundles, we end up with $B\mathrm{Spin}(2)$ as the fiber in (7.52).

Since $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is simply connected, $B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is $2$ -connected and therefore all of its vector bundles admit spin structures. Thus, when we smash (7.52) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence

$$ MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{3}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))_{+}. $$

The Thom spectrum $(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{\mathfrak{su}(2)}$ is known as James’ “quasiprojective space” (see [Jam76]). The Anderson dual of (7.53) appears in a physics application in [DDK+25, §IV.F.].

The same Thom isomorphism applies for any $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ -oriented ring spectrum, such as $MT\mathrm{SO}$ or $\mathit{ko}$ ; if we used $\mathit{ko}$ instead of $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ in (7.53), we would obtain the cofiber sequence in (B.23).

#### Example 7.54.

In [DDK+25, §III.B.1], we study the SBLES in twisted spin bordism corresponding to the vector bundle $2L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , where $L$ denotes the tautological bundle. Since $2L$ is spin, we obtain a one-periodic family of Smith homomorphisms of the form

$$ S(2L)\longrightarrow B\mathrm{U}(1)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2L}}\Sigma^{4}(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{2L-4}. For $k$ even we reduce to (7.55b) above; for $k$ odd, we have a very similar cofiber sequence, but the sphere bundle does not split: we obtain for the fiber $(\mathbb{CP}^{1})^{\mathcal{O}(-1)-2}\simeq\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ :

$$ MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge\mathbb{CP}^{2}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{4}MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}, $$

using the identification $MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L-2}\simeq MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ from Example 6.23. This is the complex analogue of (7.40).

#### Remark 7.58.

There is a related example where one uses $L\oplus L^{*}\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ instead of $2L$ ; the corresponding long exact sequence in twisted $\mathrm{SU}$ -bordism was studied by Conner-Floyd [CF66b, §§6, 14, 17]. When $k$ is odd, the third term in the long exact sequence, corresponding to the sphere bundle, is the bordism of manifolds with $c_{1}$ -aspherical structures or complex Wall structures, first introduced by Conner-Floyd [CF66b], and also discussed by Stong [Sto68, Chapter VIII]. Complex Wall bordism plays an important role in the calculation of $\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{SU}}$ via the Adams-Novikov spectral sequence [Nov67, §7], and has also been studied in the context of complex orientations [Buh72, PC23, Che23].

#### Example 7.59.

The unit sphere bundle to the tautological bundle $V_{n+1}\to B\mathrm{O}(n+1)$ is homotopy equivalent to the map $B\mathrm{O}(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n+1)$ . This is because $S^{n}\cong\mathrm{O}(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n)$ , so the unit sphere bundle can be described by the mixing construction

$$ S^{n}\times_{\mathrm{O}(n+1)}E\mathrm{O}(n+1)\cong(\mathrm{O}(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n))\times_{\mathrm{O}(n+1)}E\mathrm{O}(n+1)\cong E\mathrm{O}(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n)\cong B\mathrm{O}(n). $$

More generally, if $\xi_{n+1}\colon B_{n+1}\to B\mathrm{O}(n+1)$ is an unstable tangential structure and $\xi_{n}\colon B_{n}\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ is the pullback of $\xi_{n+1}$ by $B\mathrm{O}(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n+1)$ , the sphere bundle of $\xi_{n+1}^{*}V_{n+1}$ is the pullback of $S(V_{n+1})=B\mathrm{O}(n)$ by $\xi_{n+1}$ , which is $\xi_{n}$ . If you then pull $\xi_{n+1}^{*}V_{n+1}$ back across $B_{n}\to B_{n+1}$ , it splits as $V_{n}\oplus\underline{\mathbb{R}}$ , so there is a Smith cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma^{-1}B_{n}^{n-V_{n}}\longrightarrow B_{n+1}^{n+1-V_{n+1}}\longrightarrow\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B_{n+1}. $$

This cofiber sequence is due to Galatius-Madsen-Tillmann-Weiss [GMTW09, (3.3), §5]. The spectrum $\Sigma^{n}B_{n}^{n-\xi_{n}^{*}{V_{n}}}$ is often denoted $\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ .

## 8. Long exact sequence of invertible field theories

In this section, we turn to physical applications of the Smith fiber sequence (Theorem 5.1). In Section 8.1 we give a brief overview of anomalies and how they relate to invertible field theories. In Section 8.2 we review the mathematical classification of invertible field theories as Anderson dual groups of Thom spectra. In Section 8.3 we show how the Smith fiber sequence gives rise to a long exact sequence of invertible field theories (Corollary 8.20), which we call the symmetry breaking long exact sequence (SBLES). Finally, we give a mathematically-oriented introduction to our companion work [DDK+25] and a table of cross-listed examples (Table 2).

Quantum field theory is not yet completely mathematically formalized, and the applications of the Smith homomorphism in [HKT20, COSY20, DDK+25] take place at a physical level of rigor, not a mathematical one. As such, parts of this section are also only at a physical level of precision.

### 8.1. Anomalies and invertible field theories

Our homotopy-theoretic techniques in this paper apply to the classification of invertible field theories, while the physical objects we ultimately wish to study are (not necessarily invertible) quantum field theories with potentially anomalous symmetries. To apply our techniques, we take the following perspective on anomalies.2424 24 There are many things called “anomalies” in quantum field theory, and we are not claiming our definitions or approach is universal. Instead, our application is to a broad class of anomalies.

Let us first consider anomalies of symmetries. Physically, we begin with a $n$ -dimensional quantum system (such as a quantum field theory) with partition function $Z$ , as well as a symmetry group $G$ , which is usually a compact Lie group. We can couple the theory to a background $G$ -gauge field $A$ . Then, put simply, the $G$ symmetry is anomalous if the partition function evaluated on a pair of a closed $n$ -manifold $M$ and a background gauge field with connection $A$ is not gauge invariant but rather transforms with a phase. That is, under a gauge tranformation $A\mapsto A^{g}$ , the partition function transforms as

$$ Z(M,A^{g})=e^{i\alpha(M,A,g)}Z(M,A), $$

where $e^{i\alpha(M,A,g)}$ is a phase factor that cannot be cancelled by local counter-terms.

Mathematically, this means that when we evaluate the theory on a $n$ -dimensional manifold $M$ with a $G$ -principal bundle with connection $A$ , the partition function is a section of a non-trivial line bundle. The non-triviality of the line bundle is the anomaly.

To relate anomalies to invertible field theories, we use the notion of anomaly inflow: under mild hypotheses, and in all known cases, there is a local counterterm $e^{i\omega(K,A)}$ defined in one dimension higher, so that if $K$ is an $(n+1)$ -dimensional manifold with boundary and $\partial K=M$ (and $A$ extends into $K$ ), then

$$ e^{i\omega(K,A^{g})-i\omega(K,A)}=e^{i\alpha(M,A,g)}. $$

We may interpret $e^{i\omega(K,A)}$ as the partition function of an $n+1$ -dimensional invertible field theory with $G$ symmetry. It is invertible, as stacking with the $e^{-i\omega(K,A)}$ theory gives the trivial theory. Furthermore, $Z$ naturally lives at the boundary of this invertible theory, and together they are gauge invariant by Equation 8.2. Therefore we can interpret the existence of the $G$ -anomaly, which is the failure of $Z(M,A)$ to be gauge invariant, as the statement that $Z$ is a boundary theory of a non-trivial $(n+1)$ -dimensional invertible field theory, which we call the bulk theory. This perspective, formulated mathematically by Freed-Teleman [FT14], is the link between anomalies and invertible field theories; see also Freed [Fre23].

We also study anomalies of families of field theories parameterized by a topological space $X$ . An anomaly of an $X$ -family of field theories indicates a failure of the partition function to be consistently defined over the space of background $X$ -fields.2525 25 Typically in physics, $X$ carries more structures, such as a smooth structure or Riemannian metric. The anomalies we consider here will not depend on those structures. In this case, the bulk theory is an one-dimension-higher $X$ -family of invertible field theories. More generally, we can ask for $X$ to be a space with $G$ -action, and consider anomalies of $G$ -equivariant $X$ -families field theories. We refer the reader to [DDK+25, §II.A] and the references therein for more detail.

### 8.2. Invertible field theories and Thom spectra

Here we review the mathematical classification of (reflection-positive) invertible theories. First we must relate symmetries and tangential structures.

#### 8.2.1. Symmetries and tangential structures

For any tangential structure in the sense of Definition 2.3, there is a notion of topological field theory. Given a field theory whose anomaly we want to investigate, which tangential structure $\xi$ do we want our invertible field theories to carry?2626 26 For non-topological invertible field theories, there is also the question of enriching the tangential structure to something more geometric, such as including the data of a Riemannian metric or a connection for a principal bundle. At the level of invertible field theories this is accounted for by working with Anderson duals of bordism spectra, so our calculations include these geometric modifications.

The answer typically depends only on the symmetries of our field theory, not on its field content (the anomaly itself—which invertible field theory we get out of all the invertible field theories on $\xi$ -manifolds—uses more information from the theory). We follow Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §2], who take the stance that since we typically study QFTs in Minkowski signature but invertible field theories are Euclidean, we should Wick-rotate the group of symmetries to define our tangential structure.

Assume the dimension $n$ is at least $2$ . Let $\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ be the isometry group of Minkowski space, and let $\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}\subset\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ be the subgroup of isometries that preserve the direction of time. The group of symmetries of our theory is a Lie group $\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)$ with a map $\rho(n)\colon\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)\to\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}$ . Let $K\coloneqq\mathrm{ker}(\rho(n))$ ; we assume $K$ is compact. Assume that the normal subgroup of translations $\mathbb{R}^{1,n-1}\subset\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ lifts to a normal subgroup of $\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)$ , and let $H(1,n-1)\coloneqq\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)/\mathbb{R}^{1,n-1}$ . Now:

$$  $$

- (1) Let $\mathrm{O}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}\coloneqq\mathrm{O}(1,n-1)\cap\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ . There is an exact sequence (8.3a)

$$ 0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow H(1,n-1)\longrightarrow\mathrm{O}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}. $$

- (2) This exact sequence can be extended to an exact sequence of complexifications: (8.3b)

$$ 0\longrightarrow K(\mathbb{C})\longrightarrow H(n,\mathbb{C})\longrightarrow\mathrm{O}(n,\mathbb{C}), $$

- (3) and then to compact real forms of these complex Lie groups: (8.3c)

$$ 0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow H(n)\longrightarrow\mathrm{O}(n). $$

The tangential structure that the anomaly field theory has is $\xi\colon BH(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ . Just as it is not a priori clear that the anomaly field theory extends to dimension $n+1$ , it is also not necessarily clear that $\xi$ extends to an $(n+1)$ -dimensional unstable tangential structure, but Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 2.19] prove that it does in nearly every situation one might want, as we discuss below. In this paper, we will always be in the situation that $\xi$ extends to $(n+1)$ -manifolds.

In practice, one can often use an idea of Stehouwer [Ste22] to compute $\xi$ using the formalism of fermionic groups (sometimes called supergroups).

#### Definition 8.4 (Benson [Ben88, §7]).

A fermionic group is a topological group $G$ together with data of:

- • a central element squaring to $1$ , which we call fermion parity and denote $-1\in G$ , and

- • a group homomorphism $\theta\colon G\to\mathbb{Z}/2$ such that $\theta(-1)=0$ .

We think of $\theta$ as defining a $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -grading on $G$ , and we refer to elements of $G$ as odd or even. The even elements form a subgroup $G_{0}\subset G$ , which is itself a fermionic group with $\theta$ trivial.

Given two fermionic groups $G$ and $H$ , one can take their fermionic tensor product (ibid.) $G\otimes H\coloneqq(G\times H)/\langle(-1,-1)\rangle$ . This is a fermionic group, with central element $(-1,1)=(1,-1)$ and grading $\theta((g,h))$ equal to the sum mod $2$ of the gradings on $g$ and on $h$ .

Fermionic groups describe symmetries of theories with fermions: $-1$ acts by fermion parity, which may mix nontrivially with other symmetries in the theory; and $\theta$ describes whether elements of $G$ act unitarily or antiunitarily. Given a fermionic group $G$ , Stolz [Sto98, §2.6] defines a tangential structure $\xi_{G}\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ as follows: let $H$ be the even subgroup of the fermionic tensor product $\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\otimes G$ ; here, to make $\mathrm{Pin}^{+}$ into a fermionic group, we use the usual $-1$ , and the grading homomorphism is $\pi_{0}\colon\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\to\mathrm{O}(1)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Then $B\coloneqq BH$ , and the map $\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ is induced from the usual map $\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\to\mathrm{O}$ and the constant map to the identity on the quotient of $G_{0}$ by fermion parity. See [Ste22] for several examples of computations of tangential structures from data of the symmetries of a theory.

Tangential structures can encode not only the symmetries of quantum systems, but also the parameter space. For example, $S^{1}$ -families of fermionic theories with an internal unitary $\mathbb{Z}/2$ symmetry may be described using the tangential structure $B\mathrm{Spin}\times B\mathbb{Z}/2\times S^{1}\to B\mathrm{Spin}\to BO$ . There are also variations and twists: if $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $S^{1}$ , then we replace $B\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times S^{1}$ with the homotopy quotient $S^{1}/(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ . To encode a time-reversal symmetry $T$ with $T^{2}=(-1)^{F}$ , we replace $B\mathrm{Spin}\times B\mathbb{Z}/2$ with $B{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}$ . Note that the process of describing the symmetry and parameter space of a field theory can be subtle. See [DDK+25] for more examples of converting the data of symmetries and parameter spaces to tangential structures.

#### 8.2.2. Invertible field theories and bordism invariants

At this point in the story we have turned the physics question of determining the possible anomalies of a theory with a given collection of symmetries into the mathematical question of classifying (reflection-positive) invertible field theories for a fixed tangential structure $\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ , with $B=BG$ .

In this subsubsection we discuss how this classification question reduces to a well-studied problem in algebraic topology: the computation of groups of bordism invariants. See Freed [Fre19, Lectures 6–9] and Galatius [Gal21] for more detailed reviews of this story.

Fix nonnegative integers $k\leq n$ ; $n$ will be the dimension of the field theories we consider and $k$ will be the category number. Let $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ denote the bordism $k$ -category of $\xi$ -manifolds, whose objects are closed $(n-k)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -manifolds, morphisms are ( $\xi$ -diffeomorphism classes rel boundary of) compact $(n-k+1)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -structured bordisms between them, $2$ -morphisms are ( $\xi$ -diffeomorphism classes rel boundary of) $(n-k+2)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -structured bordisms between bordisms, and so on; see [Lur09, CS19] for more details. We will also fix a symmetric monoidal (weak) $k$ -category $\mathsf{C}$ . The motivating cases, when $k=1$ , are the categories $\mathsf{Vect}$ and $\mathsf{sVect}$ of complex vector spaces, resp. super vector spaces, with tensor product as the symmetric monoidal structure.

Following Atiyah [Ati88] and Segal [Seg88], by a field theory we mean a symmetric monoidal functor $Z\colon\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}\to\mathsf{C}$ ; the dimension of this theory is $n$ .

#### Definition 8.5 (Freed-Moore [FM06, Definition 5.7]).

An $n$ -dimensional field theory $Z\colon\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}\to\mathsf{C}$ is invertible if there is some other theory $Z^{-1}$ such that $Z\otimes Z^{-1}$ is the trivial theory.

This tensor product is evaluated “pointwise,” meaning that $(Z\otimes Z^{-1})(M)\coloneqq Z(M)\otimes Z^{-1}(M)$ , where $M$ is an object, morphism, etc. in the bordism category; therefore invertibility implies that $Z$ , as a functor, factors through the Picard sub- $k$ -groupoid of units $\mathsf{C}^{\times}$ inside $\mathsf{C}$ , meaning that if $X$ is any object, morphism, or higher morphism in $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ , $Z(X)$ is invertible: $\otimes$ -invertible if $X$ is an object, and composition-invertible if $X$ is a (higher) morphism. If $X$ is invertible, then we must have data of an isomorphism $Z(X^{-1})\xrightarrow{\cong}Z(X)^{-1}$ because $Z$ is symmetric monoidal; thus, even if $X$ is not invertible, we can heuristically define $Z(X^{-1})\coloneqq Z(X)^{-1}$ as if $X^{-1}$ existed. These definitions are compatible as $X$ varies, in the sense that $Z$ extends to the Picard $k$ -groupoid completion $\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}{}_{n}^{\xi}$ of $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ : the Picard $k$ -groupoid defined by formally adding inverses to all objects, morphisms, higher morphisms, etc. of $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ . Thus, an invertible field theory $Z\colon\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}\to\mathsf{C}$ is equivalent data to a morphism of Picard $k$ -groupoids

$$ Z\colon\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}{}_{n}^{\xi}\longrightarrow\mathsf{C}^{\times}. $$

So to compute deformation classes of invertible field theories, we should compute the groups of symmetric monoidal functors between these Picard $k$ -groupoids, modulo natural isomorphisms. The homotopy theory of Picard groupoids embeds in the usual stable homotopy category: if $\mathsf{D}$ is a Picard groupoid, the geometric realization $\lvert N\mathsf{D}\rvert$ of the nerve of $\mathsf{D}$ has an $E_{\infty}$ -structure arising from the monoidal product on $\mathsf{D}$ , and the Picard condition implies $\lvert N\mathsf{D}\rvert$ is grouplike. Therefore it is equivalent data to a connective spectrum $\lvert\mathsf{D}\rvert$ , which we call the classifying spectrum of $\mathsf{D}$ . This turns out to be a complete invariant of Picard $k$ -groupoids.

#### Theorem 8.7 (Stable homotopy hypothesis (Moser-Ozornova-Paoli-Sarazola-Verdugo [MOP+22])).

There is an equivalence of $\infty$ -categories between the $\infty$ -category of Picard $k$ -groupoids and the $\infty$ -category of spectra whose homotopy groups vanish outside of $[0,k]$ .

#### Remark 8.8.

For $k=1$ , the stable homotopy hypothesis was originally a folklore theorem: proofs or sketches appear in [BCC93, HS05, Dri06, Pat12, JO12, GK14]. For $k=2$ , the stable homotopy hypothesis was proven by Gurski-Johnson-Osorno [GJO19].

Therefore we need to compute the group of homotopy classes of maps of spectra $\lvert\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}{}_{n}^{\xi}\rvert\to\lvert\mathsf{C}^{\times}\rvert$ . A reasonable first step would be to identify these two classifying spectra. For the domain, the Picard $k$ -groupoid completion of the bordism category, this is due to Galatius-Madsen-Tillmann-Weiss [GMTW09] and Nguyen [Ngu17] for the bordism $(\infty,1)$ -category and to Schommer-Pries [SP24] for more general $(\infty,k)$ -categories.

#### Theorem 8.9 (Galatius-Madsen-Tillmann-Weiss [GMTW09], Nguyen [Ngu17], Schommer-Pries [SP24]).

If $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ denotes the $(\infty,k)$ -category of bordisms of $\xi_{n}$ -structured manifolds in dimensions $n-k,\dotsc,n$ , then there is a natural equivalence $\lvert\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}_{n}^{\xi}\rvert\simeq\Sigma^{k}\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ .

Here $\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ is a Madsen-Tillmann spectrum as in Definition 2.17.

Freed-Hopkins-Teleman [FHT10] then applied this result to classify invertible field theories in terms of $\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ . For that, one needs to determine $\lvert\mathsf{C}^{\times}\rvert$ , which of course depends on the choice of $\mathsf{C}$ —Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §5.3] argue that the (shifted) character dual of the sphere spectrum $\Sigma^{n}I_{\mathbb{C}^{\times}}$ is a universal choice, and that a related object called the (shifted) Anderson dual of the sphere spectrum $\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ should appear when one wants to classify deformation classes of invertible field theories. For applications to anomalies, we are interested in deformation classes, so use $\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ .

The Anderson dual $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ is characterized by its universal property that for any spectrum $\mathcal{X}$ , there is a short exact sequence [And69, Yos75]

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\pi_{n+1}\mathcal{X},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[\mathcal{X},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(\pi_{n+2}\mathcal{X},\mathbb{Z})}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{0.}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi} $$

We are interested in anomalies of unitary QFTs, hence we expect the anomaly theories to satisfy the Wick-rotated analogue of unitarity: reflection positivity. Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §7.1, §8.1] define reflection positivity for invertible TFTs using $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -actions on $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ and $\mathsf{C}$ ,2727 27 The definition of reflection positivity for extended not-necessarily-invertible TFTs is still open: see [JF17, FHJF+24, Ste24, MS25] for work in this direction. and prove two key results allowing for a complete classification of reflection positive invertible TFTs following their definition.

#### Theorem 8.11 (Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 2.19]).

If $n\geq 3$ and $\xi_{n}\colon BH(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ is a tangential structure arising from a representation $\rho\colon H(n)\to\mathrm{O}(n)$ with $H(n)$ a compact Lie group and $\mathrm{SO}(n)\subset\mathrm{Im}(\rho)$ , then there is a stable tangential structure $\xi\colon BH\to B\mathrm{O}$ such that $\xi_{n}$ is the pullback of $\xi$ along $B\mathrm{O}(n)\to B\mathrm{O}$ .

#### Theorem 8.12 (Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 5.23], Grady [Gra23]).

Suppose $\xi\colon BH(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 8.11. The abelian group of deformation classes of $n$ -dimensional, reflection positive invertible field theories on manifolds with $\xi$ -structure is naturally isomorphic to $[\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$ .

So after we require reflection positivity, the classification changes from unstable bordism to bordism in the usual sense, which is easier to calculate.

#### Remark 8.13.

There are some other approaches to the classification of invertible topological field theories, due to Yonekura [Yon19], Rovi-Schoenbauer [RS22], and Kreck-Stolz-Teichner (unpublished; see [Sto18]).

Theorem 8.12 has a nice interpretation from the point of view of anomalies. Using the defining property of $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ , there is a short exact sequence

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\Omega_{n+1}^{\xi},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(\Omega_{n+2}^{\xi},\mathbb{Z})}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{0,}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi} $$

where $\mathrm{Tors}(\text{--})$ denotes the torsion subgroup. Using the Pontrjagin-Thom theorem (Theorem 2.18) to interpret $\Omega_{k}^{\xi}$ geometrically as $\xi$ -manifolds modulo bordism, the first and third terms in this short exact sequence have anomaly-theoretic interpretations.

- • The quotient $\Hom(\Omega_{n+2}^{\xi},\mathbb{Z})$ is a free abelian group consisting of characteristic classes of $(n+2)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -manifolds; under this identification, the map $\psi$ sends an anomaly field theory to the corresponding anomaly polynomial, which is one degree higher, such as Chern-Simons and Chern-Weil forms. This data is visible to perturbative techniques, and is sometimes called the local anomaly.

- • The subgroup $\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\Omega_{n+1}^{\xi},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))$ is identified with the torsion subgroup of $[\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$ ; these are the reflection positive invertible field theories which are topological. Such field theories’ partition functions are bordism invariants, and the identification of these reflection positive invertible TFTs with $\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\Omega_{n+1}^{\xi},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))$ assigns to a reflection positive invertible TFT its partition function. Typically this data is invisible to perturbative methods and is called the global anomaly.

Yamashita-Yonekura [YY23] and Yamashita [Yam23] relate the short exact sequence (8.14) to a differential refinement of $\mathrm{Map}(\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}})$ .

### 8.3. Long exact sequence of invertible field theories

Just as the map of spectra of Section 3.2 induces a Smith homomorphism on bordism, it dually induces a map of invertible field theories. Explicitly, we obtain this by mapping into the Anderson dual and taking homotopy groups. As in Section 3.1, consider a topological space $X$ , a tangential structure $\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ , a virtual bundle $V\to X$ , and a vector bundle $W\to X$ of rank $r$ . As we discussed in the end of Section 8.2.1, the tangential structure encodes both symmetries of the theory as well as the parameter space.

#### Definition 8.15.

The defect anomaly map, generalized from [HKT20] section 4.2, is the map

$$ I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k-r}_{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Def}_{W}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k}_{\xi}(X^{V}) $$

of invertible field theories induced by the zero section map.

Physically, we interpret $I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k}_{\xi}(X^{V})$ to be classifying anomalies of QFTs in dimension $k-1$ with symmetry according to a $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure. The group mapping in, $I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k-r}_{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})$ , classifies the anomalies of defect theories in dimension $k-r-1$ . These defect theories are created from the bulk theory, physically, by setting a non-trivial boundary condition on a symmetry-breaking order parameter, which corresponds to a section of the vector bundle $W$ . See [DDK+25, §III.A] for further explanation.

For clarity, we begin a running example.

#### Example 8.17.

Recall the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ family of examples from Example 7.8 and specifically Equation 7.9d:

$$ MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

Here, we take $\xi$ according to spin bordism and twist with the tautological line bundle $W=\sigma$ over $X=B\mathbb{Z}/2$ . We take $V=3\sigma$ and apply the results of Section 6 to simplify (i.e., we use the fact that $4\sigma$ is spin). The corresponding map on invertible field theories is

$$ I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega_{\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2}^{k-1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Def}_{\sigma}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega_{{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}}^{k}. $$

Physically, we begin with a field theory with a pin+ symmetry; that is, a fermionic theory with an additional time reversal symmetry $T$ that squares to fermion parity: $T^{2}=(-1)^{F}$ . We require the physical assumption that there is a $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -odd bosonic operator $\phi$ such that the theory is gapped when the theory is deformed by $\phi$ . One example is the Majorana mass term for $2+1$ D Majorana fermions (see [DDK+25, §III.A.1]). We can define the theory on any manifold $M$ with a pin+ structure $P\colon M\to B{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}$ on its tangent bundle. If we choose generic configuration for the $\phi$ field, i.e., choose a section of the tautological line bundle $P^{*}\sigma$ , we arrive at an effective theory whose excitations are localized at the zero set of $\phi$ . We view this as a theory in one dimension lower, which is called a domain wall theory. Note that the bordism class of the zero set of $\phi$ is precisely the image of $[M]$ under $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ in (8.18). The domain wall theory no longer has the symmetry of the bulk theory: instead, it is a fermionic theory with a unitary internal symmetry $U$ squaring to $1$ ; i.e. it has $\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ tangential structure. We direct the reader to [DDK+25, §III.A] and [HKT20, §3.1] for more details.

In this context, anomaly matching refers to the process of identifying pairs of preimages and images of anomaly classes under the defect anomaly map $\mathrm{Def}_{W}$ . To perform anomaly matching, we must understand not only the two groups classifying the possible bulk and defect theories, but also the kernel and cokernel of the map $\mathrm{Def}_{W}$ . In some cases, one may deduce that information from an understanding of explicit bordism generators, but in general this approach is difficult. To address this question, we derived the map of spectra and identified its fiber, forming the Smith fiber sequence of Section 5. Now, just as for bordism, we may form a long exact sequence.

#### Corollary 8.20.

Applying $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ to the cofiber sequence (5.3), we obtain the following long exact sequence of Anderson-dualized bordism groups, or in light of Theorem 8.12, groups of invertible field theories:

The $\mathbb{Z}/16$ classifies anomalies of Majorana fermions in $2+1$ dimensions. An associated domain wall theory often has $1+1$ d chiral fermion modes. To answer the question of what particular chiral fermions can live on the domain wall, we need to identify the map $\mathrm{Def}_{\sigma}$ in (8.23). ## Appendix A The Long Exact Sequence in Bordism

In this appendix, we explicitly describe the Smith long exact sequence of bordism groups and work through an example. As in Section 5, let $(X,\xi)$ be a stable tangential structure, let $V$ be a virtual bundle over $X$ , and let $W$ be a real vector bundle over $X$ of rank $r$ . The corresponding long exact sequence of bordism groups of Corollary 8.20 is

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dots\to\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(X^{V})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\xi}_{k-r}(X^{V+W-r})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\xi}_{k-1}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})\to\cdots} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sm}_{W}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta} $$

Here, $p\colon S_{X}(W)\to X$ is the projection, $\mathrm{sm}_{W}$ is the Smith homomorphism, and $\delta$ is the connecting map. In this section, we will be explicit about taking the pullback $p^{*}V$ of $V$ to $S_{X}(W)$ .

Starting from the left, $\Omega_{k}^{\xi}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})$ is the bordism group of $k$ -manifolds $M$ equipped with a map $f\colon M\to S_{X}(W)$ together with a $\xi$ -structure on $TM\oplus f^{*}(p^{*}V)$ . Next, $\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(X^{V})$ is the bordism group of $k$ -manifolds equipped with a map to $X$ with the analogous twisted $\xi$ -structure, and $\Omega_{k-r}^{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})$ is the bordism group of $(k-r)$ -manifolds $N$ equipped with a map $g$ to $X$ with a $\xi$ -structure on $TM\oplus g^{*}V\oplus g^{*}W$ . Note that the Smith homomorphism lowers the dimension by $r$ and twists the tangential structure condition by $W$ .

Now we describe each map at the level of manifolds.

- (1) $p$ : Let $M$ be a closed $k$ -manifold equipped with a map $h\colon M\to S_{X}(W)$ such that $TM\oplus h^{*}V$ has a $\xi$ -structure, so that $M$ represents a bordism class in $\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})$ . The image of $M$ under $p$ is represented by the same manifold $M$ with an $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure given by the composition with the projection. That is, equip $M$ with the map $M\overset{h}{\longrightarrow}S_{X}(W)\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}X$ .

- (2) $\mathrm{sm}_{W}$ : Now let $M$ be a closed $k$ -manifold equipped with a map $f\colon M\to X$ such that $TM\oplus f^{*}V$ has a $\xi$ -structure. Let $s\colon M\to W$ be a generic section, which is transverse to the zero section $s_{0}$ . Then, the intersection $N\coloneqq s(M)\pitchfork s_{0}(M)$ is a $(k-r)$ -dimensional manifold. Let $g$ be the composite $g\colon N\hookrightarrow M\overset{f}{\to}X$ . Since the normal bundle $\nu$ to $N$ satisfies $\nu\cong f^{*}W|_{N}=g^{*}W$ , $TM|_{N}\cong TN\oplus\nu\cong TN\oplus g^{*}W$ , and hence $N$ carries an $(X,V+W)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure coming from the $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure on $M$ . We have $\mathrm{sm}_{W}\colon M\mapsto N$ .

- (3) $\delta$ : This is the connecting map in the long exact sequence. Start with a closed $k-r$ -manifold $N$ with an $(X,V+W)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure given by, as above, $g\colon N\to X$ and a $\xi$ -structure on $TN\oplus g^{*}V\oplus g^{*}W$ . Consider the sphere bundle $S_{N}(g^{*}W)$ of $W$ restricted to $N$ : it has a map to $S_{X}(W)$ given by inclusion. We claim that $S_{N}(g^{*}W)$ is the image under $\delta$ of $N$ , but it remains to show that $S_{N}(g^{*}W)$ has the appropriate tangential structure. This will be a corollary of a general splitting result of tangent bundles of sphere bundles. Lemma A.2. For any vector bundle $\pi\colon V\to B$ , there is an isomorphism of vector bundles, canonical up to a contractible space of choices, (A.3)

$$ TS(V)\oplus\underline{\mathbb{R}}\xrightarrow{\cong}\pi^{*}(TB)\oplus\pi^{*}(V). $$

For any fiber bundle $\pi\colon E\to B$ of smooth manifolds, the choice of connection splits $TE$ as a direct sum of the horizontal subbundle, which is isomorphic to $\pi^{*}(TB)$ , and the vertical tangent bundle $T_{v}E=\mathrm{ker}(\pi_{*})$ , which when pulled back to a fiber is the tangent bundle of that fiber. $$ TS(V)\oplus\nu\cong\pi^{*}(TB)\oplus T_{v}S(V)\oplus\nu\cong\pi^{*}(TB)\oplus\pi^{*}(V), $$

## Appendix B Computation of a Cobordism Euler Class

To compute the Smith homomorphism, it often suffices to take a Poincaré dual of the $\mathbb{Z}$ - or $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -cohomology Euler class of a vector bundle $V\to X$ , for example in [KTTW15, COSY20, HKT20]. However, our general definition (Definition 4.27) of the Smith homomorphism instead uses the (possibly twisted) $\xi$ -cobordism Euler class, tying more closely with invertible field theories. In this appendix, we walk through a concrete, low-dimensional example of a cobordism Euler class that goes beyond the cohomological approximation.

Recall that a spinh structure is a $(B\mathrm{SO}(3),V_{3})$ -twisted spin structure, where $V_{3}\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is the tautological vector bundle. Then, as we discussed in (7.49a), there is a Smith homomorphism

$$ \mathrm{sm}_{V}\colon\Omega_{k}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\to\Omega_{k-3}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3)). $$

#### Theorem B.2.

Give $S^{4}$ the spinh structure whose $\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ -bundle is classified by either map $S^{4}\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ whose homotopy class generates $\pi_{4}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\cong\mathbb{Z}$ .

- (1) Exactness of the Smith long exact sequence forces $\mathrm{sm}_{V}(S^{4})$ to be the bordism class of $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ with constant map to $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ in $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ .

- (2) $e(V)\in H^{3}(S^{4};\mathbb{Z})=0$ , and there is no way to assign every smooth representative of the Poincaré dual of $e(V)$ a spin structure whose bordism class equals that of $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ .

- (3) The spin cobordism Euler class of $V$ is nonzero, and all smooth representatives of its Poincaré dual have the spin bordism class of $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ and a constant map to $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ .

This is why the cohomology Euler class does not suffice in this example.

We work with $\xi=\mathrm{Spin}$ and its twists throughout this appendix; see Remark B.36 for other tangential structures. Let $\mathit{ko}$ denote the connective real $K$ -theory spectrum; work of Anderson-Brown-Peterson [ABP67] shows that the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro map $MT\mathrm{Spin}\to\mathit{ko}$ [ABS64] is $7$ -connected, meaning that as long as we restrict to manifolds of dimension $7$ and below, we may replace twisted spin bordism with twisted $\mathit{ko}$ -homology; in particular, we will work with $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology Euler classes.

Another consequence of the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro map is that vector bundles with spin structure are oriented for $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology, meaning that if $V\to X$ is a spin vector bundle, the Euler class $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)$ that a priori lives in $\mathit{ko}^{r}(X^{V-r})$ in fact can be passed by the Thom isomorphism to $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)\in\mathit{ko}^{r}(X)$ .

We will compute these Euler classes by using a formula for the Thom class in equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory. Recall that the Clifford algebra $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded $\mathbb{R}$ -algebra on $n$ odd generators $e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n}$ that anticommute and each square to $1$ ; likewise $\mathit{C\ell}_{-n}$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded $\mathbb{R}$ -algebra on $n$ anticommuting odd elements $e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n}$ , each squaring to $-1$ . See Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro [ABS64] for more on Clifford algebras.

When discussing modules, tensor products, Morita equivalence, etc. for Clifford algebras, we will always consider the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -grading and take the Koszul sign rule into account. We will use $\hat{\otimes}$ to denote this $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded tensor product.

Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $(X,A)$ a pair of $G$ -spaces such that $X/A$ is compact. Then, following Karoubi [Kar68, Kar02], we will represent classes in $\mathit{KO}_{G}^{n}(X)$ as (equivalence classes of) $G$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ -module bundles over $X$ equipped with a $G$ -invariant trivialization over $A$ .

#### Theorem B.3 (Atiyah [Ati68, Theorem 6.1]).

Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, $X$ be a compact $G$ -space, and $V\to X$ be an $8k$ -dimensional spin $G$ -equivariant vector bundle. Let $\mathcal{S}\to X$ denote the associated spinor bundle. Let $u\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{0}(V,V\setminus 0)$ be the class obtained from the $G$ -equivariant Clifford module bundle associated to $\mathcal{S}$ by the method of Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro [ABS64, §11]. Then the $G$ -equivariant Thom class of $V$ is $U_{G,V}\coloneqq w^{-k}u\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{8k}(V,V\setminus 0)$ , where $w\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{-8}(\mathrm{pt})$ is the Bott class.

Recall the exceptional isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ , and recall that $\mathit{ko}^{*}\cong\mathbb{Z}[\eta,v,w]/(2\eta,\eta^{3},2v,4w-v^{2})$ with $\lvert\eta\rvert=-1$ , $\lvert v\rvert=-4$ , and $\lvert w\rvert=-8$ .3232 32 The negative grading is a feature of generalized cohomology: for any spectrum $E$ , $E^{k}(\mathrm{pt})=E_{-k}(\mathrm{pt})=\pi_{-k}(E)$ .

The following result is stated without proof by Davis-Mahowald [DM79, §2]; see Bruner-Greenlees [BG10, Theorem 5.3.1] for a proof.

#### Proposition B.4.

There is an isomorphism of $\mathit{ko}^{*}$ -modules $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[[p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}]]$ with $\lvert p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\rvert=4$ .

The class $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ is called the first symplectic $\mathit{ko}$ -Pontrjagin class. The specific isomorphism in Proposition B.4 can be fixed uniquely by requiring that the image of $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ under $\mathit{ko}\to H\mathbb{Z}$ is the usual first symplectic Pontrjagin class, which is positive on the tautological quaternionic line bundle over $\mathbb{HP}^{1}$ .

Given a rank- $3$ spin vector bundle $V\to X$ , let $\mathcal{S}_{V}\to X$ be the associated spinor bundle, which is the quaternionic line bundle associated to the accidental isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ . We will show how the following result is a corollary of Theorem B.3.

#### Corollary B.5.

Let $V\to X$ be a rank- $3$ vector bundle with spin structure. Then $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(V)\in H^{3}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ and $e^{\mathbb{Z}/2}(V)\in H^{3}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ both vanish, and

$$ e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)=\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}_{V})\in\mathit{ko}^{3}(X). $$

We thank an anonymous referee for help with the following proof.

#### Proof sketch of Corollary B.5.

We first make two reductions.

- (1) The connective covering map $\mathit{ko}^{3}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2})\to\mathit{KO}^{3}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2})$ is an isomorphism: since $B\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ is $2$ -connected, all maps $B\mathrm{SU}_{2}\to\Sigma^{3}\mathit{KO}$ factor through the $2$ -connected cover of $\Sigma^{3}\mathit{KO}$ , which is $\Sigma^{3}\mathit{ko}$ . The connective cover map $\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{KO}$ sends Euler classes to Euler classes; therefore it suffices to show $e^{\mathit{KO}}(V)=\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S})$ (where here we abuse notation and let $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ denote its image in $\mathit{KO}$ -cohomology).

- (2) We can reduce further to a question in the $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory of a point. Specifically, the Atiyah-Segal completion theorem [AS69, Corollary 2.2] (see also [AH61]) identifies the “Borelification” map (B.7)

$$ \mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{*}(\mathrm{pt})\longrightarrow\mathit{KO}^{*}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2}) $$

as completion at a certain ideal, so if we can produce preimages of $e^{\mathit{KO}}(V)$ and $\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S})$ under (B.7), then show that they are equal, this will suffice to finish the proof.

Given a compact Lie group $G$ and a $d$ -dimensonal real spin $G$ -representation $W$ , let $e_{G}^{\mathit{KO}}(W)\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{d}(\mathrm{pt})$ denote the $G$ -equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -Euler class, defined to be the pullback of the equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory Thom class $U_{G,W}\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{d}(W,W\setminus 0)$ under the zero section. Atiyah [Ati68, §6] shows that the Atiyah-Segal completion map sends $U_{G,W}$ to the nonequivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory Thom class of the associated bundle $W\to BG$ ,3333 33 We thank Yigal Kamel for help with this point. so the analogous fact is true for Euler classes: the image of $e_{G}^{\mathit{KO}}(W)$ under (B.7) is $e^{\mathit{KO}}(W)\in\mathit{KO}^{d}(BG)$ .

Let $\mathbf{2}$ denote the defining representation of $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ and $[\mathbf{2}]$ denote its class in $\mathit{RSp}(\mathrm{SU}_{2})\cong\mathit{KSp}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{0}(\mathrm{pt})\cong\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{4}(\mathrm{pt})$ .3434 34 The notation $\mathbf{2}$ means that this representation is two-dimensional over $\mathbb{C}$ ; we work over $\mathbb{R}$ , so think of $\mathbf{2}$ as four-dimensional. Bruner-Greenlees [BG10, Theorems 5.3.1 and 5.3.5] show that $2-[\mathbf{2}]$ is a preimage of $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S})$ under the completion map. To summarize, it now suffices to show that $e_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{\mathit{KO}}(V)=\eta(2-[\mathbf{2}])$ in $\mathit{KO}^{3}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}(\mathrm{pt})$ .

To proceed, we reduce this to a purely algebraic question. As mentioned above, we may represent elements of $\mathit{KO}_{G}^{n}(\mathrm{pt})$ as equivalence classes of finite-dimensional real vector spaces with commuting $G$ -representation and $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ -module structures, and we may represent elements of $\mathit{KO}_{G}^{n}(W,W\setminus 0)$ as $G$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ -module bundles over $W$ , equipped with $G$ -invariant trivializations on $W\setminus 0$ . Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro [ABS64, §5] show that $\eta\in\mathit{KO}^{-1}(\mathrm{pt})$ is represented by $\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}$ as a module over itself; giving this module the trivial $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action produces a representative of $\eta\in\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{-1}(\mathrm{pt})$ . Thus, $\boldsymbol{2}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}$ (with $\boldsymbol{2}$ regarded as purely even) is a $\mathit{C\ell}_{4}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}$ -module. For $1\leq m\leq n$ , there is a Morita equivalence

$$ \mathsf{Mod}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}}\overset{\simeq}{\longrightarrow}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}} (\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m},\mathit{C\ell}_{n-1}) M(n,m)\coloneqq\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\underbracket{\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\dotsm\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}}_{\text{$m$ copies}}, $$

with bimodule data given by:

- • $e_{1}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}1,\dotsc,e_{n-m}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}1\in\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}$ act by left multiplication by $e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n-m}$ on $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}$ , tensored with the identity on the $\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}$ factors.

- • $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}$ acts by right multiplication on $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}$ tensored with the identity on the $\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}$ factors.

- • $e_{n-m+i}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}1\in\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}$ acts on the left by the identity on $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-1}$ tensored with $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ factor of $\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}$ , and the identity on the remaining factors.

- • $1\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}e_{i}\in\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}$ acts on the left by the identity on $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}$ tensored with $\begin{pmatrix}\phantom{-}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ factor of $\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}$ , and the identity on the remaining factors.

This Morita equivalence follows from the standard isomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded algebras $\mathit{C\ell}_{1}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}\cong\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1})$ (see, for example, [DG18, Lemma 6.17]).

Specializing to $n=4$ and $m=1$ , and giving this bimodule the trivial $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action, we see that the class $[\boldsymbol{2}]\eta\in\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{3}(\mathrm{pt})$ is represented by the $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{3}$ -module

$$ (\boldsymbol{2}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1})\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{4}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}}M(4,1). $$

For the Euler class, we use Atiyah’s Theorem B.3 identifying the $G$ -equivariant Thom class of an $8k$ -dimensional spin vector bundle. Apply this to $V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}$ , an $8$ -dimensional $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -representation, thought of as an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant vector bundle over $\mathrm{pt}$ . Since $B\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ is $3$ -connected, all $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -representations $\rho$ are spin, as $w_{2}(\rho)\in H^{2}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2};\mathbb{Z}/2)=0$ . Therefore we learn from Theorem B.3 that the Thom class $U\coloneqq U_{\mathrm{SU}_{2},V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}}$ of $V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}$ is, as an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{8}$ -bundle, constructed by Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro’s method [ABS64, §11] from the spinor representation $\mathcal{S}$ of $\mathrm{Spin}_{8}$ restricted by the standard inclusion $\mathrm{SU}_{2}\cong\mathrm{Spin}_{3}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Spin}_{8}$ . Thus we have an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{8}$ -module bundle

$$ U\in\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{8}(V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5},(V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5})\setminus 0)\cong\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{8}(\Sigma^{5}(V,V\setminus 0)). $$

The suspension isomorphism identifies this group with $\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{3}(V,V\setminus 0)$ ; to see this in terms of Clifford modules, use the trivial $\mathbb{R}^{5}$ summand of $V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}$ to define a $\mathit{C\ell}_{-5}$ -action on $U$ in a similar manner to [BE23, §4.1]. The fiber $U_{0}$ over $0\in V$ is therefore a $(\mathit{C\ell}_{8}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-5})$ -module with commuting $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action. Now use the Morita equivalence (B.8a) with $n=8$ and $m=5$ , and give the bimodule $M(8,5)$ implementing this Morita equivalence the trivial $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action. Then $U_{0}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{8}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-5}}M(8,5)$ is an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{3}$ -module, hence defines a class in $\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{3}(\mathrm{pt})$ .

What remains is a tedious but straightforward computation to identify the classes of these two $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{3}$ -modules. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem B.2.

Recall from (7.49a) that the Smith homomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{V}\colon\Omega_{k}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\to\Omega_{k-3}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ belongs to a long exact sequence whose third term is spin $c$ bordism:

$$ \dotsb\to\Omega_{2}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\to\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\to\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\overset{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}{\to}\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\to\Omega_{3}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\to\dots $$

From Stong [Sto68, Chapter XI] we know $\Omega_{3}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}=0$ and $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , from Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 9.97] we know $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , and from Wan-Wang [WW19, §5.5.3] we know $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\Omega_{2}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ is torsion. Plugging this into (B.11), we see that $\mathrm{sm}_{V}$ is surjective.

Wan-Wang’s argument implies that the map $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}\to\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ choosing the trivial $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle is an isomorphism, so the generator of $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ is any nonbounding spin $1$ -manifold with trivial $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle. Hu [Hu23, Appendix A] shows that $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ and $S^{4}$ generate $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}$ , where $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ has spinh structure induced from its spin $c$ structure via the standard inclusion $\mathrm{U}(1)\cong\mathrm{SO}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ , and $S^{4}$ has spinh structure whose principal $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle $V\to S^{4}$ is induced from the tautological quaternionic line bundle on $\mathbb{HP}^{1}\cong S^{4}$ : this has an associated $\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ -bundle, and we quotient by $\{\pm 1\}$ to get an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle. In particular, $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ is in the image of $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\to\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}$ , so because $\mathrm{sm}_{V}$ is surjective, $\mathrm{sm}_{V}(S^{4},V)$ must be $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ with trivial map to $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ , proving the first part of the theorem.

Because $H^{3}(S^{4};\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{3}(S^{4};\mathbb{Z}/2)$ both vanish, the $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/2$ cohomology Euler classes of $V$ are zero. Therefore any null-homologous $1$ -manifold in $S^{4}$ (i.e. any closed, oriented $1$ -manifold mapping to $S^{4}$ ) is a smooth representative of the Poincaré dual of $e(V)$ . Most of these manifolds, such as the standard $S^{1}\subset S^{4}$ , can be given a nonbounding spin structure, but the empty submanifold cannot, even though it is Poincaré dual to $e(V)$ . This proves the second part of the theorem.

As discussed above, the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro map is $7$ -connected, and therefore for discussing degree- $3$ spin cobordism of $S^{4}$ , we may use $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology without losing information. The Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence quickly implies

$$ \mathit{ko}^{*}(S^{4})\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[z]/(z^{2}),\ \lvert z\rvert=4. $$

In particular, $\mathit{ko}^{3}(S^{4})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ , generated by $\eta z$ .

The spinor bundle of $V$ is the quaternionic line bundle associated to the identification $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ . Since $V$ came from the identification $S^{4}\cong\mathbb{HP}^{1}$ , the spinor bundle of $V$ is the tautological quaternionic line bundle $L_{\mathbb{H}}\to\mathbb{HP}^{1}$ . This is classified by the inclusion $j\colon\mathbb{HP}^{1}\to\mathbb{HP}^{\infty}\simeq B\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ as the $4$ -skeleton; considering the map of Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences for $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology induced by $j$ shows that $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ pulls back by $j$ to $z\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(S^{4})$ . Thus by Corollary B.5, $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)=\eta z\neq 0$ in $\mathit{ko}^{3}(S^{4})$ .

Because $\mathit{ko}^{3}(S^{4})$ has only one nonzero element, the Poincaré dual of the nonzero element must be the unique nonzero element $x$ of $\mathit{ko}_{1}(S^{4})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Pulling back to spin bordism, the same argument we made for $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ shows that the smooth representatives of $x$ are precisely the nonbounding spin $1$ -manifolds with null-bordant map to $S^{4}$ —and composing with the map $S^{4}\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ classifying $V$ , we have shown that every smooth representative of the Poincaré dual of $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)$ (hence also the spin cobordism Euler class) represents the image of $(S^{4},V)$ under the Smith homomorphism. ∎

Using the Wood cofiber sequence (B.21), any one of these three results implies the other two; we will prove (2).

Restricted to $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ , $y$ is a map

A map of $\mathit{ko}$ -modules $\Sigma^{m}\mathit{ko}\to\Sigma^{n}\mathit{ku}$ is equivalent data to a map of spectra $\Sigma^{m}\mathbb{S}\to\Sigma^{n}\mathit{ku}$ , which is classified by $\pi_{n}(\mathit{ku})$ . Since $\mathit{ku}$ is connective, all “off-diagonal terms” vanish unless $4k+2\geq 4\ell+2$ ; therefore for our $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ summand we may restrict to the map

$$ y\colon\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ko}\vee\dotsb\vee\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ku}\vee\dotsb\vee\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ku}. $$

We may therefore describe $y$ as a $(k+1)\times(k+1)$ matrix. Connectivity of $\mathit{ku}$ implies this matrix is upper triangular.

We saw in (B.27) that if $m\geq\ell$ , then $\pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathit{ko}}(\Sigma^{4m+2}\mathit{ko},\Sigma^{4\ell+2}\mathit{ku})\cong\pi_{2(m-\ell)}\mathit{ku}\cong\mathbb{Z}$ ; tracing through the identifications there, we learn that this $\mathbb{Z}$ of maps is the set of scalar multiples of the map $b^{2(m-\ell)}c$ , where $b\colon\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ku}\to\mathit{ku}$ is the connective version of the Bott periodicity map. Therefore there are integers $\lambda_{ij}$ for $1\leq i<j\leq k+1$ such that the map (B.28) is given by the following upper triangular matrix:

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\pm c&\lambda_{12}b^{2}c&\lambda_{13}b^{4}c&\dotsb&\lambda_{1(k+1)}b^{2k}c\\
&\pm c&\lambda_{23}b^{2}c&\dotsb&\lambda_{2(k+1)}b^{2k-2}c\\
&&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\
&&&\pm c&\lambda_{k(k+1)}b^{2}c\\
&&&&\pm c\end{bmatrix}. $$

This matrix can clearly be row-reduced over $\mathit{ko}_{*}$ to $c\cdot\mathrm{Id}$ , and the requisite row operations correspond to automorphisms of $\mathit{ko}\vee\dotsb\vee\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ . The row operations are compatible with adding on more summands by increasing $k$ , so we may conclude. ∎

#### Lemma B.30 (Bruner-Greenlees (see [BPR23, Theorem 3.8])).

Recall $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[[p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}]]$ from Proposition B.4. There is an isomorphism $\varphi\colon\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathit{ko}_{*}[x]$ , where $\lvert x\rvert=4$ ,3636 36 Here we use polynomial notation only for conciseness; we have not defined any ring structure on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ . such that the $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ -module structure on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ is the one uniquely specified by

$$ p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\frown x^{k}=x^{k-1}. $$

Finally, we can calculate the $\mathit{ko}$ -Euler class!

#### Proof of Corollary B.5.

It suffices to work universally with the tautological bundle $V_{3}\to B\mathrm{Spin}(3)$ ; the spinor bundle is the tautological quaternionic line bundle associated to $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ , and so $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}_{V_{3}})$ is the class we called $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ in Proposition B.4.

By Proposition B.24,

$$ e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{3})\frown x^{k}=\eta x^{k-1}, $$

where we define $x^{-1}=0$ for convenience.3737 37 As we have not been careful about explicit choices of isomorphisms, there could be a sign factor in the choice of $x^{k}$ , but since $2\eta=0$ , the possible sign error goes away. A general element of $\mathit{ko}^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ is of the form

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}\eta(p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}})^{k}w^{k-1}. $$

We know how $\eta$ and $w^{k-1}$ act on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ because the $\mathit{ko}$ -theory cap product is linear over $\mathit{ko}^{*}$ . We know how $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ acts on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ thanks to Lemma B.30. Using these, we can see that the only class of the form (B.33) whose cap product matches that of $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{3})$ in (B.32) is $\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ .

Finally, we have to check that $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(V_{3})$ and $e^{\mathbb{Z}/2}(V_{3})$ both vanish. $B\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ is $3$ -connected, so $H^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1);\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1);\mathbb{Z}/2)$ both vanish. ∎

#### Remark B.34 (Euler classes of low-rank spin vector bundles).

For $2\leq n\leq 6$ , $\mathrm{Spin}(n)$ participates in an accidental isomorphism with another Lie group, and one can run similar arguments to compute $\mathit{ko}$ -Euler classes of other low-rank vector bundles as corollaries of Atiyah’s Theorem B.3.

- (1) If $L$ is a real line bundle with spin structure, $e^{\mathit{ko}}(L)=0$ , because $e^{\mathit{ko}}$ pulls back from the twisted Euler class over $B\mathrm{SO}(1)=*$ ; see, e.g., Crabb [Cra91, Corollary 3.37(i)].

- (2) If $V_{2}$ has rank $2$ , one can use the accidental isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(2)\cong\mathrm{U}(1)$ and the fact that the map $c\colon\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{U}(1))\to\mathit{ku}^{*}(B\mathrm{U}(1))$ is injective [BG10, §5.2] to show that $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{2})$ is determined by $e^{\mathit{ku}}(V)$ , hence also by $e^{K}(V)$ , the image in periodic $K$ -theory. In particular, $V_{2}$ acquires the structure of a complex line bundle, and there is a formula for the $K$ -theory Euler classes of complex vector bundles, e.g. in Bott [Bot69, (7.2)].

- (4) If $V_{4}\to X$ has rank $4$ , its spinor bundle factors as $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}^{+}\oplus\mathcal{S}^{-}$ , where the two factors $\mathcal{S}^{\pm}$ are quaternionic line bundles associated to the two factors of $\phi\colon\mathrm{Spin}(4)\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{Sp}(1)\times\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ . There is a choice of $\phi$ such that (B.35)

$$ e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{4})=p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}^{+})-p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}^{-})\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(X). $$

- (5) There is an accidental isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(5)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(2)$ , and $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(2))\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[[p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}},p_{2}^{\mathbb{H}}]]$ with $\lvert p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\rvert=4$ and $\lvert p_{2}^{\mathbb{H}}\rvert=8$ (see [DM79, §2] or [BG10, Theorem 5.3.5]). Therefore $\mathit{ko}^{5}(B\mathrm{Sp}(2))\cong 0$ , so for any rank- $5$ spin vector bundle $V_{5}$ , $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{5})=0$ ; see, e.g., Crabb [Cra91, Corollary 3.37(i)].

#### Remark B.36.

We saw above that for twisted spin bordism, the $\mathit{ko}$ -theoretic Euler class suffices to approximate the cobordism Euler class. For other tangential structures, one may need more or less information.

- • Unoriented bordism decomposes as a sum of shifts of mod $2$ homology, and this splitting is compatible with the Smith homomorphism. Therefore in this setting, one can use the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -cohomology Euler class.

- • Wall [Wal60] showed that $MT\mathrm{SO}$ , localized at $2$ , splits as a sum of shifts of $H\mathbb{Z}$ and $H\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Therefore when one studies Smith homomorphisms for twisted oriented bordism, the $\mathbb{Z}$ -cohomology Euler class will be accurate up to odd-primary torsion. On odd-primary torsion, oriented and spin bordism coincide, so in that setting one can use $\mathit{ko}$ -Euler classes for twisted oriented bordism.

- • Analogously to spin and $\mathit{ko}$ , one can use $\mathit{ku}$ -theory Euler classes for twisted spin $c$ bordism Smith homomorphisms.
